discovery:
Actinium was discovered in 1899 by French chemist **André-Louis Debierne** while he was working with
            the Curies on a residue from pitchblende, the same ore from which they discovered polonium and radium. He
            named it "actinium" from the Greek word *aktinos*, meaning "**ray**" or "**beam**," because of its intense
            radioactivity. It was also independently discovered in 1902 by Friedrich Oskar Giesel, who named it
            "emanium," but Debierne's name was officially adopted.
uses:
Actinium has no significant commercial applications. Its primary use is in **scientific research**,
                where
                it is used as a powerful source of alpha particles.

The radioisotope **Actinium-225** is currently being researched for use in **targeted alpha therapy**,
                a new form of cancer treatment that uses the potent alpha radiation to destroy cancer cells with minimal
                damage to surrounding healthy tissue.
It can also be used as a neutron source in certain specialized laboratory settings.
interestingFacts:
Actinium is a soft, silvery-white metal that is extremely radioactive. It is about **150 times more
                radioactive than radium**.

Due to its intense radioactivity, actinium glows faintly in the dark with a pale blue light, which is
                produced by the ionization of the surrounding air by its emitted particles.

Actinium is the first element of the actinide series, a group of 15 elements with similar chemical
                properties, which is named after it.
didYouKnow:
The intense radioactivity of actinium makes it a powerful source of alpha particles, which can be used to
            produce neutrons. In equilibrium with its decay products, a sample of actinium can be a more powerful source
            of radiation than a similar amount of radium.

Discovered in the 1750s by Andreas Marggraf, first isolated as metal by Hans Christian Ørsted in 1825.
            Mass production began in 1886 via the Hall‑Héroult process. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

Packaging (foil, cans), wiring, cookware
Alloys (e.g. duralumin) for strength and lightweight

It has low density—about one‑third that of steel. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}
didYouKnow: Aluminium plays vital roles in aviation and packaging, and is fully recyclable with minimal degradation.

color: Silvery-white, tarnishes slowly in dry air
discovery:
Americium was discovered in 1944 by a team of scientists led by **Glenn T. Seaborg** at the University of
            Chicago. It was one of the first transuranic elements to be synthesized. They produced it by bombarding
            plutonium with neutrons. The new element was named in honor of the **Americas**, in analogy to europium
            which was named after the continent of Europe.
uses:
The most common and widespread use of americium is in **household smoke detectors**. The isotope
                **Americium-241** is the active component.

It is also used as a portable gamma ray source for industrial gauges, such as those used to measure
                the thickness of glass, paper, and metal sheets.
Americium is used as a source of neutrons for well logging applications in the oil and gas industry.
interestingFacts:
Americium is a highly radioactive and toxic heavy metal. Its most common isotope, Am-241, has a
                half-life of
                432 years.
It is one of the very few synthetic elements with a common household use.
Americium is a dense, silvery-white metal that tarnishes slowly in dry air.
didYouKnow:
A tiny amount of Americium-241, often less than 1 microgram, is the key component inside most household
            smoke detectors. It emits alpha particles that ionize the air in a chamber, allowing a small electric
            current to flow. When smoke enters the chamber, it disrupts this current, triggering the alarm.

discovery:
Antimony has been known since ancient times. Its compounds were used in cosmetics, medicine, and as an
            alloying agent. The first detailed description of the preparation of antimony metal was published in 1540 by
            the German metallurgist Vannoccio Biringuccio, but the element was likely known much
            earlier. The name "antimony" is thought to derive from the Greek words "anti" and "monos," meaning "not
            alone," referring to its presence in various compounds. Its symbol, Sb, comes from the Latin word
            "stibium."
uses:
The most important use of antimony is as a hardening alloy for lead, particularly in lead-acid batteries
                for vehicles.
Antimony compounds are used as flame retardants in plastics, textiles, and other materials.
It is a component in certain solders and low-friction alloys (babbitt metal) used in bearings.

Antimony sulfide is used as a pigment in paints and plastics and in the tips of "strike-anywhere"
                matches.
In the semiconductor industry, antimony is used as a dopant for silicon to create n-type semiconductors.
interestingFacts: Antimony is a brittle, silvery-white semimetal with a layered crystal structure.
It has multiple allotropes, with the metallic form being the most stable.
Historically, antimony sulfide was used as kohl (a type of eyeliner) in ancient Egypt.
Antimony is a toxic element, and its compounds can cause health issues if ingested or inhaled.
didYouKnow:
The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder referred to antimony sulfide as "stibium," which is where the element's
            chemical symbol, Sb, originates.

discovery:
Discovered in 1894 by Lord Rayleigh and Sir William Ramsay while studying nitrogen from air. It was the first
            noble gas discovered.
uses: Used as an inert shielding gas in welding and other high-temperature processes
Fills incandescent and fluorescent light bulbs
Used in double-pane windows as an insulating layer
interestingFacts: Argon is chemically inert and does not form compounds easily
It gets its name from the Greek word "argos" meaning lazy or inactive
Despite being inert, it glows violet in electric discharge tubes
didYouKnow:
Argon was originally considered to be a contaminant in nitrogen experiments until its identity as a new
            element was confirmed.

discovery:
Arsenic has been known since ancient times in various compounds. The element itself is attributed to
            Albertus Magnus (Albert the Great) in the 13th century, who described its isolation.
uses:
Historically used in pesticides, herbicides, and wood preservatives (e.g., chromated copper arsenate),
                though these uses have been largely phased out due to toxicity concerns.

Used in semiconductors, particularly in gallium arsenide (GaAs) for high-speed electronic devices,
                infrared devices, and optoelectronics.
In small quantities, used to harden lead alloys for car batteries and ammunition.
Certain arsenic compounds are used in specialized glass production.
Arsenic trioxide is used in some medical treatments, particularly for certain types of leukemia.
interestingFacts: Arsenic is famously known for its toxicity, and it has been used as a poison throughout history.
It exists in several allotropic forms, with metallic grey arsenic being the most stable.
When heated in air, arsenic quickly oxidizes, emitting a garlic-like odor.
didYouKnow:
Despite its notorious toxicity, arsenic compounds have medicinal applications. For example, arsenic trioxide
            is used in chemotherapy for acute promyelocytic leukemia, demonstrating the complex nature of elements and
            their biological interactions.

discovery:
Astatine was discovered in 1940 by American physicists **Dale R. Corson**, **Kenneth Ross MacKenzie**, and
            **Emilio Segrè**. They synthesized it by bombarding bismuth-209 with alpha particles (helium nuclei) at the
            University of California, Berkeley's cyclotron. They named it "astatine" from the Greek word *astatos*,
            meaning "**unstable**," because of its very short half-life and extreme radioactivity.
uses:
The radioisotope **Astatine-211** is used in **targeted alpha particle therapy** for cancer treatment.
                Its
                potent alpha radiation and short half-life make it a highly effective and precise tool for destroying
                cancer cells with minimal damage to surrounding healthy tissue.

Astatine is also used in a variety of scientific research applications, particularly in radiochemistry
                and nuclear medicine.
interestingFacts:
Astatine is so rare and unstable that its bulk physical properties are largely unknown. Many of its
                properties, such as its color and melting point, are estimated based on its position in the periodic
                table as a halogen.
Its most stable isotope, Astatine-210, has a half-life of only 8.1 hours.

As a halogen, it is expected to have some non-metallic properties, but due to its high atomic mass, it
                is also believed to exhibit some metallic characteristics.
didYouKnow:
If you could magically gather all the astatine that exists naturally on Earth at a single moment, it would
            be so small an amount that it would likely fit inside a cube no larger than a few millimeters on each side.

discovery:
Barium was first identified as a new element in 1774 by Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm
                Scheele
            in a new mineral he discovered. However, it was not isolated as a pure metal until 1808, when English
            chemist
            Sir Humphry Davy produced it through the electrolysis of molten barium compounds. Davy
            named the element "barium" from the Greek word "barys," meaning "heavy," because of the high density of its
            mineral, barite.
uses:
Barium sulfate is used as a radiocontrast agent for medical imaging of the gastrointestinal tract, known
                as a "barium meal."

It is a key component in the drilling fluids used in oil and gas wells, helping to increase the density
                of the fluid to prevent blowouts.
Barium nitrate and barium chlorate are used to produce the green color in fireworks.
Barium is used as a getter in vacuum tubes and as a component in alloys for spark plugs.
Barium titanate is an important component in some capacitors and piezoelectric ceramics.
interestingFacts: Barium is a very reactive metal and is always found in nature in its combined state.

While barium sulfate is safe for use in medical imaging because of its low solubility, most other
                barium compounds are highly toxic and can cause heart problems and paralysis.

The mineral barite is famously known as a "heavy spar" because of its high density, which is about four
                times that of water.
didYouKnow:
The use of barium sulfate in medical imaging is a classic example of a "chemical paradox." A compound
            containing a highly toxic element is used safely because the specific compound is insoluble and therefore
            not absorbed by the body.

discovery:
Berkelium was discovered in 1949 by a team of scientists led by **Glenn T. Seaborg** at the University of
            California, Berkeley. They synthesized it by bombarding a sample of americium-241 with alpha particles
            (helium nuclei). The element was named after the city of **Berkeley**, California, where it was discovered,
            in analogy to terbium, which was named after the Swedish town of Ytterby.
uses: Berkelium has **no commercial uses** due to its extreme radioactivity, scarcity, and short half-life.

Its primary use is in **scientific research**, particularly in the synthesis of even heavier,
                transuranic elements.

The isotope **Berkelium-249** is used as a target material to create new elements, such as tennessine,
                element 117.
interestingFacts:
Berkelium is a highly radioactive and toxic heavy metal. Its most stable isotope, Berkelium-247, has a
                half-life of 1,380 years.
It was the fifth transuranic element to be synthesized.

Due to its rarity, the first visible sample of berkelium was only a microscopic quantity, and its
                properties were determined using extremely sensitive techniques.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of berkelium was a key stepping stone in the creation of the transuranic elements. By using
            berkelium as a target, scientists were able to synthesize even heavier and more exotic elements in
            particle accelerators.

discovery:
Beryllium was discovered in 1798 by French chemist Louis Nicolas Vauquelin in beryl and
            emeralds. It was later isolated as a metal by Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy in 1828.
uses: Used in aerospace materials due to its lightweight and stiffness
Used in X-ray windows due to transparency to X-rays
Used in nuclear reactors as a moderator and reflector
Added to copper and other alloys to improve hardness
interestingFacts: Beryllium is highly toxic if inhaled as dust or fumes
It has one of the highest melting points among light metals
It has a high stiffness-to-weight ratio
Its name is derived from the mineral "beryl"
didYouKnow:
Beryllium is used in the James Webb Space Telescope's mirrors because it can withstand the extreme cold of
            space while maintaining its shape and performance.

discovery:
Bismuth has been known since ancient times, but it was often confused with lead and tin due to its similar
            physical properties. It was first formally recognized as a distinct element in 1753 by the French chemist
            **Claude-François Geoffroy**, who demonstrated that it was different from both lead and tin.
uses:
The primary use of bismuth is as a component in **low-melting-point alloys** that are often used as
                a replacement for toxic lead in solders, plumbing, and fire sprinklers.

**Bismuth subsalicylate** is the active ingredient in many common stomach remedies, such as
                Pepto-Bismol.

Bismuth compounds are used in **cosmetics**, particularly in eye shadows and nail polishes, where they
                provide a pearlescent sheen.
It is used in some catalysts for the production of synthetic fibers and rubber.

Bismuth is also being investigated as a potential component in nuclear fuel and as a non-toxic
                alternative
                to lead in shotgun pellets.
interestingFacts:
Bismuth is the **heaviest non-radioactive element**, which is a distinction it has held for a long time.
                However, its most common isotope, Bismuth-209, is now known to be radioactive with an extremely long
                half-life (longer than the age of the universe), so it is considered stable for all practical purposes.

When melted bismuth cools and solidifies, it forms stunning, iridescent, hopper-shaped crystals. This
                unique property makes it a popular material for hobbyists and collectors.
Bismuth has a very low thermal conductivity and is a strong diamagnetic material.
didYouKnow:
Bismuth is one of the few elements that **expands as it solidifies**, a property it shares with water.
            This makes it useful in some alloys for producing very sharp castings with intricate details.

discovery:
Bohrium was discovered in 1981 by a German research team led by **Peter Armbruster** and **Gottfried
            Münzenberg** at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt. They synthesized it by
            bombarding a bismuth-209 target with chromium-54 ions. The element was named in honor of the Danish
            physicist **Niels Bohr**, a pioneer of atomic structure theory.
uses:
Bohrium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Bohrium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Bohrium-270, has a half-life of only about 61 seconds.

It is named after a person who was not involved in its discovery, which was a departure from previous
                naming conventions.

Bohrium is predicted to have chemical properties similar to its lighter homologues in Group 7, such
                as rhenium and manganese.
didYouKnow:
Due to the short half-life of its isotopes, experiments involving bohrium must be performed quickly and on
            a single-atom basis. This makes the study of its chemical properties a remarkable feat of experimental
            science.

discovery:
Boron was discovered independently by Sir Humphry Davy, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, and Louis Jacques Thénard in
            1808 through the electrolysis of borates.
uses: Used in glass and ceramics (borosilicate glass).
Essential in fertilizers for plant growth.
Used in detergents and cleaning agents.
Used in neutron absorbers in nuclear reactors.
interestingFacts: Boron is a metalloid – it has properties of both metals and non-metals.
It's vital in small amounts for plant and possibly human health.
Boron fibers are strong and used in advanced aerospace materials.
didYouKnow:
Boron nitride is nearly as hard as diamond and used in abrasives and cutting tools. Boron also helps regulate
            hormone levels in the human body!

discovery:
Bromine was independently discovered by two chemists in 1826: Antoine Jérôme Balard in
            France and Carl Jacob Löwig in Germany. Balard published his findings first and named it
            bromine, from the Greek word "bromos," meaning "stench."
uses: Used in fire retardants for plastics and textiles.
In agriculture as a fumigant for pest control (e.g., methyl bromide, though usage is declining).
Historically used in photography as silver bromide (AgBr) in photographic films and papers.
Bromine compounds are used in water purification and as disinfectants.
Used in some specialized drilling fluids.
interestingFacts: Bromine is the only nonmetallic element that is liquid at room temperature.
It is highly corrosive and toxic, especially in its vapor form.
Bromine has a distinctive, strong, and unpleasant odor.
It reacts readily with many elements and organic compounds.
didYouKnow:
The intense red-orange color of liquid bromine and its reddish-brown vapor make it one of the most visually
            striking elements on the periodic table. Its name, meaning "stench," aptly describes its strong and
            disagreeable odor.

color: Silvery-white metal with a bluish tinge
discovery:
Cadmium was discovered in 1817 by German chemist Friedrich Stromeyer. He was examining zinc
            carbonate for its purity when he found an impurity that was a new element. He named it after the Latin word
            "cadmia" and the Greek word "kadmeia," both ancient names for calamine (zinc carbonate).
uses:
Historically, a major use of cadmium was in rechargeable nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cd) batteries, but this is
                declining due to its toxicity.

Cadmium compounds were used to create bright yellow, orange, and red pigments for paints and plastics,
                often known as "cadmium yellow" or "cadmium red."

It has been used in electroplating to provide a protective, corrosion-resistant coating for steel and
                other metals.

Cadmium is a key component in cadmium telluride (CdTe) solar panels, which are an important type of
                thin-film solar technology.
Due to its ability to absorb neutrons, it is used in control rods in some nuclear reactors.
interestingFacts: When a bar of pure cadmium is bent, it emits a crackling sound, similar to that of tin.

Cadmium and its compounds are highly toxic and exposure can cause serious health problems, including
                cancer and kidney damage.

The use of cadmium in many products is being phased out in many parts of the world due to its
                environmental and health risks.
didYouKnow:
The famous "Itai-Itai" disease in Japan was caused by chronic cadmium poisoning from industrial pollution
            that contaminated rice fields. The disease led to severe bone pain and fractures.

discovery:
Pure calcium was isolated by Sir Humphry Davy in 1808 via electrolysis of its oxide, though calcium compounds
            (lime) were used since ancient times :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}.
uses: Used in steelmaking as deoxidizer and desulfurizer.
Calcium compounds are used in cement, plaster, and building materials.
Used in dietary supplements and antacids.
interestingFacts: Essential for bone and tooth health in living organisms.
Bright yellow‑red flame test indicates calcium presence.
Name derives from Latin “calx” meaning lime :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}.
didYouKnow: Calcium is used in automotive batteries as alloying element to reduce maintenance and improve safety.

discovery:
Californium was discovered in 1950 by a team of scientists led by **Glenn T. Seaborg** at the University
            of California, Berkeley. They synthesized it by bombarding a tiny sample of curium-242 with alpha particles
            (helium nuclei). The element was named after the state of **California** and the university where the
            discovery was made.
uses:
The primary use of californium is as a powerful **neutron source**. The isotope **Californium-252**
                is a strong neutron emitter through spontaneous fission.

This neutron source is used in a variety of applications, including **neutron activation analysis** to
                detect elements in materials, moisture gauges for finding water in soil, and in portable metal
                detectors.
In medicine, californium-252 is used for treating certain types of **tumors** in radiotherapy.
It is also used to start nuclear reactors.
interestingFacts:
Californium-252 is one of the most powerful neutron emitters known. A single microgram of the isotope
                can
                produce millions of neutrons per second.
It is so rare and expensive that it is typically sold by the microgram.
Due to its intense radioactivity, handling californium requires extensive safety precautions.
didYouKnow:
A tiny amount of Californium-252, about the size of a pinhead, can emit millions of neutrons per second.
            This
            makes it an ideal portable neutron source for a variety of industrial and medical applications where a
            compact and powerful source of neutrons is needed.

discovery:
Carbon has been known since ancient times in the form of charcoal and soot. It was recognized as an element
            in the 18th century.
uses: As a fuel (coal, petroleum).
In steel production.
As graphite in pencils and lubricants.
As diamonds in cutting tools and jewelry.
In electronics and nanotechnology (graphene, carbon nanotubes).
interestingFacts: Carbon forms more compounds than any other element.
It's essential to life — present in proteins, fats, DNA, and sugars.
Carbon dating is used to determine the age of archaeological samples.
didYouKnow:
Graphene, a form of carbon just one atom thick, is 200 times stronger than steel and conducts electricity
            better than copper!

discovery:
Cerium was discovered in 1803 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth and,
            independently, by Swedish chemists Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm
                Hisinger.
            Klaproth named the new element after the dwarf planet Ceres, which had been discovered just two years
            earlier. The new element was found in the mineral cerite, which was later named after the element itself.
uses:
Cerium is a key component in **catalytic converters for automobiles**, where it helps reduce carbon
                monoxide (CO) emissions.

In the form of mischmetal, an alloy of rare-earth metals, it is used to make **lighter flints** and in
                metallurgy to remove impurities from steel.

Cerium oxide is a highly effective **polishing powder for glass**, used for camera lenses, telescopes,
                and mirrors.
It is used in self-cleaning ovens as a catalyst to help burn off food residue.

Cerium is also a component in certain special glasses and alloys, including those used in lighting and
                aerospace applications.
interestingFacts:
Cerium is a highly reactive metal that tarnishes quickly in the air and can spontaneously ignite when
                scratched or heated to around 150 °C.

It is one of the few lanthanides that can exist in more than one stable oxidation state, most commonly
                +3 and +4.

The name "Cerium" is directly linked to the first-ever discovery of a celestial body via a telescope in
                1801, the dwarf planet Ceres.
didYouKnow:
The use of cerium oxide as a glass polishing agent is a major industrial application. The cerium oxide
            slurry not only mechanically abrades the glass but also chemically interacts with the surface, resulting in
            a
            smoother, higher-quality finish than other polishing compounds.

discovery:
Cesium was discovered in 1860 by German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav
                Kirchhoff. They were the pioneers of spectroscopy and discovered the element by analyzing the
            spectrum of a mineral water sample from Durkheim, Germany. They observed two bright blue lines and named the
            element "cesium" from the Latin word "caesius," meaning "sky blue."
uses:
Cesium's most famous use is in atomic clocks, which are the most accurate timekeeping devices in the
                world.

Cesium formate brines are used in the oil and gas industry as a lubricant for high-pressure drilling
                fluids.

Due to its photoelectric properties, it is used in photocells, night vision devices, and other optical
                equipment.
Cesium vapor is used in ion propulsion systems for spacecraft.
It is also used in vacuum tubes, as a getter to scavenge residual gases.
interestingFacts:
Cesium is the softest of all metals and is so reactive that it will explode on contact with water or
                even ice.
It is one of only five metals that are liquid at or near room temperature.

The official definition of a second is based on the frequency of a specific transition of the cesium-133
                atom.
didYouKnow:
The frequency of light absorbed by a cesium atom (9,192,631,770 hertz) is so precise and stable that it has
            been used since 1967 to define the length of a second, making cesium atomic clocks the foundation of modern
            timekeeping.

discovery: Discovered by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in 1774. Officially recognized as an element by Humphry Davy in 1810.
uses: Water purification and disinfection
Bleach production
Plastics (PVC)
interestingFacts: Essential for producing hydrochloric acid (HCl)
Used in making medicines and pesticides
didYouKnow: Chlorine is poisonous at high concentrations and was used as a chemical weapon in World War I.

discovery:
Chromium was discovered by French chemist Louis Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797. He isolated the element from a
            mineral known as Siberian red lead (crocoite).
uses:
Major component in stainless steel, providing its corrosion resistance and lustrous finish (e.g., in
                cutlery, kitchenware, and industrial equipment).
Used for chrome plating, which provides a hard, corrosion-resistant, and shiny surface to other metals.
Chromium compounds are used as pigments in paints (e.g., chrome yellow), ceramics, and glass.
Used in the tanning of leather.

Some chromium compounds are essential micronutrients (e.g., in glucose metabolism), though hexavalent
                chromium is toxic.
interestingFacts:
The name "chromium" comes from the Greek word "chroma", meaning "color", due to the wide variety of
                colors its compounds can exhibit.
It is the third hardest element after carbon (diamond) and boron.
Chromium plating is a very thin layer (often less than a micrometer thick).
didYouKnow:
The brilliant red color of rubies comes from trace amounts of chromium impurities within the corundum
            crystal lattice.

color: Lustrous, silver-gray metal with a bluish tint
discovery:
Cobalt was discovered by Swedish chemist Georg Brandt in 1735. He was able to prove that the blue color in
            glass, previously attributed to bismuth, was actually due to a new element, which he named cobalt.
uses: Essential component in lithium-ion batteries, especially for electric vehicles and portable electronics.

Used in the production of superalloys for jet engines and gas turbines due to its high-temperature
                strength and corrosion resistance.
Forms strong, permanent magnets (e.g., Alnico magnets).
Cobalt-60 is an important radioisotope used in medical treatments (radiotherapy) and sterilization.
Cobalt compounds are used as pigments to produce vibrant blue colors in glass, ceramics, and paints.
interestingFacts:
The name "cobalt" comes from the German word "Kobold", meaning "goblin" or "evil spirit", given by
                miners because its ores were difficult to smelt and poisoned other extracted metals.
It is one of only three naturally occurring ferromagnetic elements (the others are iron and nickel).
Vitamin B12 is the only vitamin that contains cobalt.
didYouKnow:
Due to its critical role in lithium-ion batteries and its concentrated supply in certain regions, cobalt has
            become a strategically important and highly sought-after commodity.

discovery:
Copernicium was discovered in 1996 by a German research team led by **Sigurd Hofmann** at the GSI
            Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt. They synthesized it by bombarding a lead-208 target
            with a beam of zinc-70 ions. The element was named in honor of the Polish astronomer **Nicolaus
            Copernicus**,
            who developed the heliocentric model of the solar system.
uses:
Copernicium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Copernicium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Copernicium-285, has a half-life of only about 29 seconds.
It is the heaviest known member of the Group 12 elements (zinc, cadmium, and mercury).

Theoretical predictions, due to **relativistic effects**, suggest that copernicium may be a noble
                gas-like
                element, and possibly a liquid or gas at room temperature, which is a highly unusual property for a
                metal in its group.
didYouKnow:
The estimated melting point of copernicium is so low that it could be a liquid at room temperature, making
            it a potential "super-heavy mercury" that would be extremely volatile and dangerous.

discovery:
Copper has been known and used by humans for at least 10,000 years, making it one of the oldest metals
            discovered. Its use dates back to the Neolithic period, and it was the first metal to be smelted from its
            ores.
uses: Widely used in electrical wiring due to its excellent electrical conductivity.
Used extensively in plumbing and roofing due to its corrosion resistance and malleability.

A key component in various alloys such as brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin), and
                cupronickel (copper and nickel).
Used in coinage, decorative arts, and statuary.
Essential micronutrient for living organisms.
interestingFacts: Copper is an excellent conductor of heat and electricity, second only to silver among metals.
It is naturally antimicrobial, meaning it can kill bacteria and viruses on its surface.

The Statue of Liberty is covered with a thin layer of copper, which has oxidized over time to form its
                iconic green patina.
didYouKnow:
The "Bronze Age" was a period characterized by the widespread use of bronze, an alloy of copper (typically
            with tin), for tools and weapons, demonstrating the early importance of copper in human civilization.

discovery:
Curium was discovered in 1944 by a team of American scientists led by **Glenn T. Seaborg** at the
            University of California, Berkeley. They synthesized it by bombarding a plutonium-239 target with
            alpha particles (helium nuclei). The element was named in honor of **Marie and Pierre Curie**, pioneers
            in the field of radioactivity research.
uses: Curium has **no commercial applications** outside of scientific research.

The isotope **Curium-244** is a powerful heat source from its radioactive decay. This property makes it
                a potential fuel for **radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs)**, which are used to power
                space probes.

Curium is a subject of research in nuclear physics and radiochemistry, particularly for its role in
                understanding the heavier elements.
interestingFacts:
Curium is a highly radioactive and toxic heavy metal. Its most stable isotope, Curium-247, has a
                half-life of 15.6 million years.

It is one of the most intensely radioactive elements, glowing a faint blueish-purple light due to the
                ionization of the surrounding air by its radiation.
It was the third transuranic element to be discovered.
didYouKnow:
The intense radioactivity of curium makes it a powerful heat source. Curium-242 was used to power the first
            RTG that was sent to the Moon in 1969 to provide power for scientific instruments on the Apollo 12 mission.

discovery:
Darmstadtium was discovered in 1994 by a German research team led by **Peter Armbruster** and **Gottfried
            Münzenberg** at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. They synthesized it by
            bombarding a lead-208 target with a nickel-64 beam. The element was named after the city of **Darmstadt**,
            where the discovery was made.
uses:
Darmstadtium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Darmstadtium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Darmstadtium-281, has a half-life of only about 2 minutes.

It is a very dense element, with an estimated density of about 34.8 g/cm³, which is heavier than
                all known stable elements.

Darmstadtium is the heaviest known member of the Group 10 elements, and its chemical properties are
                expected to be similar to its lighter homologues, nickel, palladium, and platinum.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of darmstadtium was a significant step in the synthesis of superheavy elements, proving that
            the periodic table continues to hold true even at the extreme end of the table. Its discovery was a testament
            to the power of particle accelerator technology.

discovery:
The discovery of dubnium was the subject of a long-standing dispute between Soviet and American
            scientists. A team at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in **Dubna**, Russia, claimed discovery in
            1967. A few years later, a team at the University of California, Berkeley, claimed their own discovery in
            1970. The name **Dubnium** was ultimately approved by the IUPAC in 1997 in honor of the Russian research
            center.
uses:
Dubnium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Dubnium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Dubnium-268, has a half-life of only about 29 hours.

It is the **first transactinide element** in Group 5 of the periodic table, showing chemical
                properties similar to tantalum.

The naming dispute over dubnium was a part of what became known as the "**Transfermium Wars**"
                between Soviet and American scientists, a period of controversy over the naming of elements 104-106.
didYouKnow:
The production of dubnium is so difficult that only a few hundred atoms have ever been synthesized.
            This makes its study a major challenge for nuclear chemists who must work with extremely short-lived,
            tiny samples of the element.

discovery:
Dysprosium was discovered in 1886 by French chemist **Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran**. He isolated it
            from a sample of holmium oxide and was the first to recognize it as a new element. He named it from the
            Greek word *dysprositos*, meaning "**hard to get**," due to the immense difficulty he had in separating it
            from the other rare-earth elements.
uses:
Dysprosium is a crucial component in high-performance **neodymium-iron-boron magnets**. Adding
                dysprosium
                significantly improves the magnets' coercivity and their ability to function at high temperatures,
                making them vital for electric vehicle motors and wind turbine generators.

It is also a key component in the alloy **Terfenol-D** (Terbium, Dysprosium, Iron), which is used in
                high-tech sonar systems and other transducers.

Dysprosium is used in **control rods for nuclear reactors** because of its high neutron absorption
                cross-section.
It is used in certain types of lasers and as a component in metal halide lamps.
interestingFacts:
Dysprosium has one of the highest magnetic moments of any element, a property that makes it invaluable
                in high-strength magnets.
It is a soft, silvery-white metal that can be cut with a knife.

Due to its importance in green technologies, dysprosium is considered a strategically important and
                critical element.
didYouKnow:
The high demand for dysprosium in powerful magnets for electric cars and wind turbines has led to it being
            one of the most expensive and sought-after rare-earth elements on the market.

discovery:
Einsteinium was discovered in 1952 by a team of scientists led by **Albert Ghiorso** at the University of
            California, Berkeley. It was found in the debris of the first **hydrogen bomb test** in the Pacific. The
            element was named in honor of the physicist **Albert Einstein**.
uses:
Einsteinium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                short
                half-life.

Its primary use is in **scientific research**, particularly in the synthesis of even heavier
                transuranic elements.

Einsteinium's properties are studied to better understand nuclear physics and the behavior of the
                actinide series.
interestingFacts: Einsteinium was the seventh transuranic element to be discovered.
The most stable isotope, Einsteinium-252, has a half-life of about 471 days.
Because of its intense radioactivity, einsteinium glows in the dark with a blue light.
The discovery was initially kept secret for years due to Cold War secrecy surrounding nuclear weapons.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of Einsteinium in the aftermath of a nuclear explosion was a testament to the power of
            scientific observation. Scientists had to quickly and carefully analyze the fallout debris to identify the
            presence of this new, highly unstable element.

discovery:
Erbium was discovered in 1843 by Swedish chemist **Carl Gustaf Mosander**. While analyzing a sample of the
            mineral gadolinite, he was able to separate the yttrium oxide component into three new elements, which he
            named terbia, erbia, and yttria. He named the element Erbium after the village of **Ytterby**, Sweden,
            the same location that also gave its name to yttrium, terbium, and ytterbium.
uses:
Erbium is a key component in **fiber optic communications**, particularly in Erbium-doped fiber
                amplifiers (EDFAs) that amplify light signals without needing to convert them to electricity.

In the medical field, **erbium-doped lasers (Er:YAG lasers)** are used for various applications,
                including
                skin resurfacing, dental surgery, and plastic surgery.
Erbium is used as a colorant in glass and porcelain enamel, where it imparts a distinct **pink color**.

Its compounds are also used in phosphors for displays and in some metallurgical applications to improve
                the ductility of metals.
interestingFacts:
Erbium is a soft, malleable, silvery-white metal that is relatively stable in air compared to other
                rare-earth metals.

The pink color produced by erbium ions in glass and crystals is a defining characteristic of the
                element.

Erbium-doped optical fibers are so efficient at amplifying light that they form the backbone of modern
                long-haul fiber optic networks, allowing data to be transmitted across oceans and continents.
didYouKnow:
The village of Ytterby, Sweden, is home to a mineral mine that has provided the source material for the
            discovery of four different elements: Yttrium, Terbium, Erbium, and Ytterbium. This makes it the most
            prolific
            single location for element discovery in the world.

discovery:
Europium was discovered in 1901 by French chemist **Eugène-Anatole Demarçay**. While examining samples of
            the rare-earth elements samarium and gadolinium, he noticed new spectral lines that indicated the presence
            of another element. He successfully isolated this new element and named it in honor of the continent of
            **Europe**.
uses:
Europium is most famously used as a **phosphor** in television screens and fluorescent lamps to produce
                the vibrant **red color**.
Europium-doped phosphors are also used in some modern LED lighting and display technologies.

The unique fluorescent properties of europium compounds are used in **anti-counterfeiting** measures,
                such as on Euro banknotes and some security inks.
Europium is a dopant in some optical glass and has been researched for use in quantum computing.
It is also being explored for applications in high-performance solar cells.
interestingFacts: Europium is the most reactive of the lanthanide elements. It oxidizes very quickly when exposed to air.
Due to its softness and high reactivity, it is one of the least dense of the rare-earth metals.

Europium's unique fluorescence, particularly its bright red color when excited by ultraviolet light, is
                a
                defining characteristic and the reason for many of its applications.
didYouKnow:
The distinct, bright red color you see on your television screen or computer monitor, especially in older
            CRT displays, is often a result of europium atoms being excited by electrons or UV light and then emitting
            a very specific wavelength of red light.

discovery:
Fermium was discovered in 1952 by a team of scientists led by **Albert Ghiorso** at the University of
            California, Berkeley. It was found in the debris of the first **hydrogen bomb test** (Ivy Mike) in the
            Pacific Ocean. The element was named in honor of **Enrico Fermi**, a pioneer of nuclear physics and the
            creator of the first nuclear reactor.
uses:
Fermium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and short
                half-life.

Its primary use is in **scientific research**, particularly in the synthesis of even heavier
                transuranic elements and in understanding the properties of the actinide series.
interestingFacts: Fermium was the eighth transuranic element to be discovered.
The most stable isotope, Fermium-257, has a half-life of about 100.5 days.

It is a highly radioactive and toxic element. The half-life of all of its isotopes is too short for it
                to be produced in macroscopic, usable quantities.
didYouKnow:
Fermium-257 is the heaviest element that can be produced by neutron capture, as the next isotope in the
            process, Fermium-258, is highly unstable and undergoes spontaneous fission almost immediately. This
            effectively marks a limit to element synthesis via neutron capture.

discovery:
Flerovium was discovered in 1998 by a Russian-American team at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research
            (JINR) in Dubna, Russia. The team was led by **Yuri Oganessian**. They synthesized it by bombarding a
            plutonium-244 target with a calcium-48 beam. The element was named in honor of the physicist **Georgy
            Flyorov**, who founded the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions at JINR.
uses:
Flerovium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Flerovium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Flerovium-289, has a half-life of only about 2.6 seconds.

It is located in the theorized "**island of stability**," which predicts that isotopes with certain
                numbers of protons and neutrons would have longer half-lives than other superheavy elements.

Theoretical predictions suggest that flerovium may be a noble gas, despite its location in the poor
                metals group, due to relativistic effects.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of flerovium was a significant step in the search for the "island of stability." Its
            relatively longer half-life compared to its neighbors provides tantalizing evidence that this island
            of stability may actually exist.

discovery:
First discovered in mineral compounds by Georgius Agricola in 16th century and hydrofluoric acid
            characterized by Scheele in 1771. Successfully isolated in elemental form by French chemist Henri
                Moissan in 1886 via electrolysis of hydrogen fluoride—earning him the Nobel Prize
            :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}.
uses: Manufacture of fluorochemicals (e.g. Teflon, refrigerants like Freon)
Water fluoridation to help prevent tooth decay
Production of high-end pharmaceuticals—≈20 % contain fluorine :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
Etching glass with hydrofluoric acid
Used in uranium enrichment and nuclear fuel processing
didYouKnow:
Despite being highly reactive and rarely found in nature, fluorine compounds such as fluoride are essential
        for dental health and modern electronics—but elemental fluorine gas itself is one of the most dangerous
        substances on Earth.

discovery:
Francium was discovered in 1939 by French chemist **Marguerite Perey** at the Curie Institute in Paris. She
            found the element as a decay product of actinium-227. Perey named the element "francium" after her home
            country, **France**.
uses: Francium has **no commercial uses** due to its extreme rarity and instability.

It is primarily used in **scientific research**, particularly in atomic spectroscopy, to study its
                atomic structure and properties.
Francium is also used in biological studies as a tracer to investigate cell functions.
interestingFacts:
Francium is the **most unstable of the first 103 elements**, with its most stable isotope, Fr-223,
                having a
                half-life of only 22 minutes.

It is the **second-most electropositive element** after cesium and is believed to have the lowest
                electronegativity of all known elements.

Because of its extreme radioactivity and short half-life, any macroscopic sample of francium would
                be vaporized by its own radioactive heat almost instantly.
didYouKnow:
Francium is so rare and short-lived that it has never been seen as a bulk liquid or solid. All observations
            of its properties are based on radio-spectroscopic measurements of very small groups of atoms.

discovery:
Gadolinium was discovered in 1880 by French chemist **Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac**. He detected the
            presence of the new element by identifying its unique spectroscopic lines in a sample of the mineral
            samarskite. He named the new element after the mineral **gadolinite**, which in turn was named in honor of
            the Finnish chemist **Johan Gadolin**, who had discovered the first rare-earth element, yttrium.
uses:
The most famous use of gadolinium is in **MRI contrast agents**. Its powerful paramagnetic properties
                enhance the image quality of internal organs and tissues, helping doctors to detect tumors and other
                abnormalities.

Gadolinium has the highest thermal neutron capture cross-section of any known element, making it useful
                in **control rods** for nuclear reactors and for shielding in neutron radiography.

It is used in a special alloy with iron and chromium to improve the workability and high-temperature
                resistance of these metals.
Gadolinium compounds are used as phosphors in color television tubes and in X-ray imaging screens.
It is also being explored for use in magnetic refrigeration technology due to the magnetocaloric effect.
interestingFacts:
Gadolinium is ferromagnetic at temperatures below 20 °C (room temperature) and is the most paramagnetic
                element above that temperature.

The name Gadolinium is a unique tribute, as it's the only element named after a person who also had a
                mineral named after them.

Despite its name, Johan Gadolin did not discover the element gadolinium itself, but a different
                rare-earth
                element in the mineral later named in his honor.
didYouKnow:
The use of gadolinium in MRI scans is so effective because of its unique magnetic properties. When injected,
            it alters the magnetic field of water molecules, causing them to show up much more brightly on the scan and
            providing a clearer, more detailed image for radiologists.

state: Solid (but melts just above room temperature)
discovery:
Gallium was predicted by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1871 and was discovered by French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de
            Boisbaudran in 1875 using spectroscopy. He named it after his native land, Gaul (Latin: Gallia).
uses:
Primary use is in gallium arsenide (GaAs) for semiconductors, LEDs, laser diodes, and solar cells due to
                its superior electronic properties compared to silicon in some applications.
Used in high-temperature thermometers because of its wide liquid range.

Forms low-melting-point alloys with other metals, which can be used in some medical and dental
                applications.
Gallium nitride (GaN) is used in blue and green LEDs, and in high-power, high-frequency devices.
interestingFacts:
Gallium is one of the few metals that can melt in the palm of your hand, as its melting point is just
                above room temperature.
It expands when it freezes, similar to water, which is unusual for metals.

Liquid gallium can "wet" glass, meaning it spreads out and sticks to the surface, making it difficult to
                clean.
didYouKnow:
Due to its low melting point and relatively low toxicity, gallium is sometimes used as a non-toxic
            alternative to mercury in some thermometers and barometers.

discovery:
Germanium was predicted by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869 (as "eka-silicon") and was discovered by German chemist
            Clemens Winkler in 1886. Winkler named the element after his home country, Germany.
uses:
Used extensively in semiconductors for transistors and diodes, especially in early electronics, though
                largely replaced by silicon.
Important for fiber optic communication cables due to its high refractive index.

Used in infrared optics, including night vision devices, thermal imaging cameras, and other optical
                instruments.
Used as a polymerization catalyst in the production of certain plastics.
Germanium alloys are used in dentistry and for some specific metal applications.
interestingFacts: Germanium is a metalloid, meaning it has properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals.
It is an important semiconductor material, allowing for control of electrical conductivity.
Early transistors were often made of germanium before silicon became dominant.
didYouKnow:
One of the critical uses of germanium is in lenses and windows for infrared optical systems because it is
            transparent to infrared radiation and has a high refractive index, making it ideal for thermal imaging.

discovery:
Gold has been known and highly valued since prehistoric times. It is one of the **"seven metals of
            antiquity"** and its discovery is not attributed to a single person. It has been used for coinage, jewelry,
            and art for thousands of years by civilizations across the globe, including ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia,
            and the Roman Empire.
uses: The primary use of gold is in **jewelry**, accounting for over 50% of the global demand.
It is also used as a **store of value** and an investment in the form of coins and bullion.

Due to its excellent electrical conductivity and corrosion resistance, gold is used in **electronics**
                for connectors, contacts, and wiring in high-end devices like computers and smartphones.
In **dentistry**, gold is used for fillings, crowns, and bridges due to its inertness and malleability.

It is used in a variety of other applications, including in medical treatments, glass production, and
                aerospace engineering.
interestingFacts:
Gold is the most malleable and ductile of all metals. A single gram of gold can be hammered into a sheet
                one square meter in size, or drawn into a wire over a mile long.

It is a noble metal, meaning it is highly resistant to corrosion, oxidation, and most acids. Only
                a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids (aqua regia) can dissolve it.

The purity of gold is measured in **karats**. 24-karat gold is 99.9% pure, while 18-karat gold is 75%
                gold and 25% other metals.
didYouKnow:
Due to its inertness and resistance to corrosion, gold is used in surgical implants and other medical
            devices
            that need to be in contact with the human body for extended periods without causing an immune response.

discovery:
Hafnium was discovered in 1923 by Dutch physicist Dirk Coster and Hungarian chemist
            George de Hevesy in Copenhagen, Denmark. Their discovery was based on Niels Bohr's atomic
            theory, which predicted an element with an atomic number of 72 would exist and have properties similar to
            zirconium. They found the element in zirconium-containing ores and named it after *Hafnia*, the Latin name
            for Copenhagen.
uses:
Hafnium is primarily used in **control rods for nuclear reactors** because of its very high capacity
                to absorb neutrons.

Its excellent corrosion resistance and high melting point make it a valuable component in superalloys
                used in the aerospace industry.

Hafnium and its compounds are used as an essential component in the gate oxide insulator of advanced
                silicon-based integrated circuits.

Hafnium carbide ($HfC$) is one of the most refractory binary compounds known and is used in plasma
                cutting electrodes.
It is also used as a getter in some vacuum tubes to scavenge oxygen and nitrogen.
interestingFacts:
Hafnium's high neutron-absorption cross-section is the opposite of zirconium's, which is very low. This
                is why they must be separated for nuclear applications; hafnium is for control rods, and zirconium is
                for fuel rod cladding.

The first sample of pure hafnium was only a few milligrams and was a byproduct of an earlier attempt to
                isolate the element.
The discovery of hafnium filled the last remaining gap in the periodic table for a stable element.
didYouKnow:
The element hafnium was the last element with a stable nucleus to be discovered. Its existence was
            theoretically predicted years before it was physically isolated, demonstrating the power of periodic law and
            atomic theory.

discovery:
Hassium was discovered in 1984 by a German research team led by **Peter Armbruster** and **Gottfried
            Münzenberg** at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. They synthesized
            it by bombarding a lead-208 target with iron-58 ions. The name **Hassium** was approved in 1997, after
            a naming dispute, and it was named after the German state of **Hesse**, where the research institute is
            located.
uses:
Hassium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Hassium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Hassium-270, has a half-life of only about 21 seconds.

It is a very dense element, with an estimated density of about 40.7 g/cm³, which would make it one of
                the densest elements in the periodic table.

Hassium is the heaviest known member of the Group 8 elements, and its chemical properties are
                expected to be similar to its lighter homologues, osmium and ruthenium.
didYouKnow:
The chemical properties of hassium have been studied on a single-atom basis. By creating volatile
            hassium tetroxide, scientists were able to determine that it behaves chemically like its lighter
            homologue, osmium, confirming the trends of the periodic table in the heaviest elements.

discovery:
Helium was first discovered in 1868 by French astronomer Jules Janssen and English
            astronomer Joseph Norman Lockyer while observing a solar eclipse.
            It was first isolated on Earth in 1895 by Scottish chemist Sir William Ramsay.
uses:
Used in cryogenics, especially as liquid helium to cool superconducting magnets (e.g., in MRI
                scanners)
Used in balloons and airships as a non-flammable lifting gas
Used in welding as a shielding gas
Used in breathing mixtures for deep-sea diving (e.g., heliox)
Used in scientific research and particle accelerators
interestingFacts: Helium is the second lightest and second most abundant element in the universe
It is completely inert and has no known chemical compounds under standard conditions
Helium is the only element that remains liquid near absolute zero without external pressure
It is used to cool the Large Hadron Collider at CERN
Inhaling helium temporarily changes the pitch of your voice (not safe in large quantities!)
didYouKnow:
Helium is a non-renewable resource on Earth. Once released into the atmosphere, it escapes into space.
            Due to increasing demand and limited supply, helium conservation is becoming an important topic.

discovery:
Holmium was discovered in 1878 by Swiss chemists **Marc Delafontaine** and **Jacques-Louis Soret**.
            Independently, it was also discovered in 1879 by Swedish chemist **Per Teodor Cleve**. Cleve was working
            with a sample of erbium oxide from the mineral gadolinite when he isolated a new element which he named
            Holmium, after **Holmia**, the Latin name for Stockholm, Sweden.
uses:
Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element, making it useful in
                **superconducting
                magnets** and as a component in certain alloys.

**Holmium-doped YAG (Ho:YAG) lasers** are used in medical and dental applications, such as for the
                ablation of soft tissue in surgery and for breaking up kidney stones.
It is also a colorant for cubic zirconia and glass, giving them a yellow or reddish color.

Holmium is used in **nuclear reactor control rods** as a burnable poison to help control the nuclear
                fission process.
interestingFacts: Holmium is a relatively soft, silvery-white metal that is malleable and ductile.

The name of the element is a tribute to Stockholm, Sweden, where the first isolation was made public by
                Cleve.

Holmium-doped YAG lasers are known for their specific infrared wavelength, which is strongly absorbed
                by water, allowing for precise cutting and cauterizing of tissue with minimal heat damage.
didYouKnow:
The most common use of holmium in modern medicine is in high-tech surgical lasers. The specific wavelength
            of light produced by these lasers is ideal for a variety of surgical procedures, from arthroscopic surgery
            to the removal of tumors.

discovery:
Hydrogen was first recognized as a distinct element by Henry Cavendish in 1766.
            He described it as "flammable air" which formed water upon combustion.
            Later, in 1783, Antoine Lavoisier named it *Hydrogen*, meaning "water-former".
uses: Production of ammonia (NH₃) using the Haber process
Used in fuel cells for clean electricity generation
Used as a rocket fuel (liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen)
Used in the hydrogenation of oils and fats
Used in metallurgy as a reducing agent
Potential energy source in hydrogen-powered vehicles
interestingFacts: Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe
It exists naturally as a diatomic molecule (H₂)
Hydrogen isotopes: Protium (¹H), Deuterium (²H), and Tritium (³H)
Stars fuse hydrogen into helium in a process that powers them
Hydrogen has metallic properties under extreme pressure
didYouKnow:
Hydrogen is the only element whose isotopes have different names:
            Protium (¹H - no neutron),
            Deuterium (²H - one neutron), and
            Tritium (³H - two neutrons, radioactive).
            Deuterium is used in nuclear reactors and research!

discovery:
Indium was discovered in 1863 by German chemists Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymous
                Theodor Richter. They were using a spectroscope to look for thallium in zinc ores and instead
            found a brilliant indigo-blue spectral line, which led them to name the new element Indium after the Latin
            word "indicum," meaning indigo.
uses:
The largest use of indium is in the production of indium tin oxide (ITO), which is a transparent
                conductive coating used in LCD displays and touchscreen devices.
It is used in low-melting-point alloys, such as those used in fire sprinkler systems.

Indium is a component in some solders used in electronics, particularly for joining non-metallic
                materials.
In nuclear reactors, indium is used in control rods due to its ability to absorb neutrons.
It is also used to make mirrors that are highly resistant to corrosion and have a high reflectivity.
interestingFacts: Indium is so soft that it can be scratched with a fingernail.
When a bar of indium is bent, it emits a high-pitched "tin cry" similar to the sound produced by tin.

The liquid range of indium is quite large, from its melting point of 156.6 °C to its boiling point of
                2072 °C, making it useful in certain high-temperature applications.
didYouKnow:
Indium tin oxide (ITO), a compound of indium, is essential for the function of modern smartphones and
            tablets. The transparent conductive layer on the screen that registers your touch is made of ITO.

color: Lustrous metallic gray-black solid; violet vapor
discovery:
Iodine was discovered in 1811 by French chemist Bernard Courtois. He was producing
            saltpeter
            for gunpowder manufacturing from seaweed ash. He noticed that when he added sulfuric acid to the ash, a
            beautiful violet vapor was produced. In 1813, the French chemist Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac
            identified this as a new element and named it "iode" after the Greek word "ioeides," meaning
            "violet-colored."
uses:
Iodine is an essential element in human nutrition, necessary for the production of thyroid hormones.
                Iodized salt is widely used to prevent iodine deficiency disorders like goiter.
In the form of tincture of iodine and povidone-iodine, it is a powerful antiseptic used to clean wounds.
Radioactive iodine-131 is used in medicine to treat thyroid cancer and hyperthyroidism.
Silver iodide is used in photography and cloud seeding to produce rain.
Iodine is also used in catalysts, dyes, and in the production of some specialty chemicals.
interestingFacts: Iodine is a halogen and is the heaviest stable halogen.

It is one of the few elements that sublimes easily, meaning it transitions directly from a solid to a
                gas without passing through a liquid phase.

The atomic number of Iodine (53) is less than the atomic number of Tellurium (52), which is an exception
                to the general trend in the periodic table.
didYouKnow:
The characteristic deep purple or violet color of iodine vapor is a defining feature of the element and is
            what gave it its name. You can see this effect by gently heating iodine crystals in a flask.

discovery:
Iridium was discovered in 1803 by English chemist **Smithson Tennant**. While working with a residue
            left over after dissolving platinum ore in aqua regia, he noticed a new, insoluble metallic element. He
            named it Iridium from the Latin word *iris*, meaning "**rainbow**," because of the wide variety of colors
            its salts exhibited in solution.
uses:
Iridium is used in **high-temperature crucibles**, especially for growing synthetic crystals used in
                electronics.

Due to its extreme durability, it is used in **spark plug tips** for aircraft engines and in certain
                high-performance electrical contacts.

An **iridium-platinum alloy** was historically used to create the standard international meter bar and
                kilogram mass, due to its resistance to corrosion and wear.

Iridium is a catalyst in certain chemical reactions and is used in a variety of specialized
                applications, including in deep-space telescopes.
interestingFacts:
Iridium is the **most corrosion-resistant metal** known to man. It is unaffected by most acids and
                alkalis.
It is the **second-densest element**, with a density of 22.56 g/cm³, just slightly less than osmium.

Iridium is a relatively common element in asteroids, and the high concentration of iridium in the
                geological layer known as the **K-T boundary** provides strong evidence for a major asteroid impact
                that led to the extinction of the dinosaurs.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of the iridium anomaly at the K-T boundary was one of the most significant scientific
            discoveries of the 20th century. This thin layer, found worldwide, contains a concentration of iridium far
            higher than what is typical for Earth's crust, pointing to an extraterrestrial origin.

discovery:
Iron has been known since ancient times. Its use by humans dates back to prehistoric times, with the
            earliest iron objects found dating from around 3200 BC in Egypt.
uses:
Primary component of steel, an essential material for construction, infrastructure, vehicles, and
                machinery.
Used in cast iron for pipes, automotive parts, and cookware.

Important in biological systems, particularly as a component of hemoglobin in blood, which carries
                oxygen.
Used in various industrial catalysts.
interestingFacts: The Earth's core is believed to be composed primarily of iron and nickel.

Pure iron is relatively soft, but its strength is dramatically increased when alloyed with carbon to
                form steel.

Iron is ferromagnetic, meaning it can be magnetized, a property crucial for many electrical
                applications.
didYouKnow:
The Iron Age, following the Bronze Age, marked a significant period in human history characterized by the
            widespread use of iron tools and weapons.

discovery:
Krypton was discovered in 1898 by Scottish chemist Sir William Ramsay and English chemist
            Morris Travers. They isolated it by fractional distillation of liquid air, alongside neon
            and xenon, and named it from the Greek word "kryptos," meaning "the hidden one."
uses:
Used in certain types of electric lights, such as fluorescent lamps, high-speed photography flashes, and
                some incandescent lights for longer lifespan and higher efficiency.
Krypton-fluoride lasers are used in nuclear fusion research.
Used in some specialized gas discharge lamps for light shows and advertising.

Because of its lower thermal conductivity, it's used as a filler gas in some double-paned windows for
                better insulation.
interestingFacts: Krypton is one of the noble gases, known for its extreme chemical inertness.

It emits a white light when an electric current passes through it, making it useful in certain lighting
                applications.

For a short period, the meter was defined by the wavelength of light emitted by Krypton-86, before being
                redefined in terms of the speed of light.
didYouKnow:
Despite its rarity, krypton has played a role in science fiction, famously as "Kryptonite" in the Superman
            comics, although the real element is a harmless noble gas and not a radioactive mineral from outer space!

discovery:
Lanthanum was discovered in 1839 by Swedish chemist Carl Gustav Mosander. He was analyzing a
            sample of cerite, a mineral from which the element cerium had been isolated. He was able to separate a new
            substance he called "lanthana," which was a mixture of rare earth oxides. He named the new element
            "lanthanum" from the Greek word *lanthanein*, meaning "to lie hidden," because it was difficult to separate
            from the other rare earth elements.
uses: Lanthanum is used in alloys to make mischmetal, a key component in **flint for lighters**.

In camera and telescope lenses, lanthanum oxide is used to create high-refractive-index glass, which
                improves image clarity and reduces aberrations.
It is a key component in nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries, widely used in hybrid vehicles.
Lanthanum oxide is used as a catalyst in petroleum cracking and as a component in ceramics and glass.

It is also used in some carbon arc lamps for studio lighting and projectors because it produces a bright,
                white light.
interestingFacts: Lanthanum is the element that gives the lanthanide series its name and serves as its prototype.

It is a soft, malleable, silvery-white metal that is highly reactive and tarnishes rapidly when exposed
                to air.
When heated in air, powdered lanthanum can ignite and burn vigorously.
didYouKnow:
The use of lanthanum in hybrid car batteries is so significant that it takes about 10 to 15 pounds of
            lanthanum to make the battery for a single Toyota Prius, making it a critical element in the green technology
            sector.

discovery:
Lawrencium was discovered in 1961 by a team of scientists led by **Albert Ghiorso** at the University of
            California, Berkeley. They synthesized it by bombarding a californium target with boron ions in a linear
            accelerator. The element was named in honor of **Ernest O. Lawrence**, the inventor of the cyclotron, a
            device that was instrumental in the discovery of many synthetic elements.
uses:
Lawrencium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and very
                short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to understand the fundamental properties of the heaviest
                elements and to test theories of nuclear and atomic structure.
interestingFacts:
Lawrencium is the **last element of the actinide series**. Its discovery completed the filling of the
                f-block in the seventh period.
The most stable isotope, Lawrencium-262, has a half-life of only about 3.6 hours.
It was the first element to be named after a person who was still living at the time of its naming.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of lawrencium was a key milestone in the synthesis of new elements. Its short half-life and
            the tiny amounts produced make it one of the most difficult elements to study, and its properties are still
            a subject of ongoing research.

discovery:
Lead has been known since ancient times and is one of the **"seven metals of antiquity"**. Its discovery is
            not attributed to a single person. Evidence of its use dates back to at least 7000 BCE in Turkey. The
            Romans used lead extensively for water pipes and other plumbing applications, which is the origin of its
            chemical symbol **Pb**, from the Latin word *plumbum*. This is also where the English word "plumber" comes
            from.
uses:
The largest use of lead is in **lead-acid batteries** for vehicles, which accounts for most of its
                global
                consumption.

Due to its high density, it is an excellent material for **radiation shielding** from X-rays and gamma
                rays, making it vital for medical and nuclear applications.

Lead is also used in the production of ammunition (bullets) and in various alloys, such as **solder**
                and
                pewter.

Historically, it was used in paint pigments and gasoline additives, but these uses have been phased
                out in most countries due to its toxicity.
interestingFacts:
Lead is a heavy, soft, and malleable metal. It is highly toxic and exposure can cause neurological
                damage, especially in children.

It is a very dense element, but it is not as dense as some other heavy metals like gold, tungsten, or
                platinum.
Lead's atomic symbol, Pb, comes from the Latin word *plumbum*, which also gives us the word "plumbing."
didYouKnow:
Despite being a known poison, lead remains an indispensable element in certain applications. Its high
            density and large atomic number are unique properties that make it highly effective at absorbing X-rays and
            gamma rays, a critical function in protecting people from radiation in medical and industrial settings.

discovery:
Lithium was discovered in 1817 by Swedish chemist Johan August Arfvedson while analyzing
            the mineral petalite.
            It was isolated in metallic form by William Thomas Brande and Humphry Davy
            shortly afterward using electrolysis.
uses: Used in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries for electronics and electric vehicles
Used as a mood stabilizer in psychiatric medicine (lithium salts)
Used in aerospace alloys due to its light weight
Used as a coolant in nuclear reactors
Used in the production of ceramics and glass
interestingFacts: Lithium is the lightest metal and the least dense solid element
It reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen gas and heat
Its name comes from the Greek word "lithos", meaning "stone"
Lithium is essential for modern battery technology and renewable energy storage
It was one of the three elements produced in the Big Bang
didYouKnow:
Lithium-ion batteries power smartphones, laptops, and electric cars.
            The demand for lithium has surged in recent years, leading to a global race for lithium mining and
            sustainable recycling technologies.

discovery:
Livermorium was discovered in 2000 by a Russian-American team at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research
            (JINR) in Dubna, Russia. The team was led by **Yuri Oganessian** and included scientists from the Lawrence
            Livermore National Laboratory in the United States. The element was named in honor of the **Lawrence
            Livermore National Laboratory** and the city of Livermore, California.
uses:
Livermorium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Livermorium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Livermorium-293, has a half-life of only about 61 milliseconds.

It is located in the theorized "**island of stability**," which predicts that isotopes with certain
                numbers of protons and neutrons would have longer half-lives than other superheavy elements.

Theoretical predictions suggest that livermorium should be a semi-metal with properties similar to
                its lighter homologue, polonium.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of livermorium, along with other superheavy elements, confirmed the trends of the periodic
            table in this extreme region and provided valuable data for the search for the "island of stability," an
            area of theoretical elements that may be relatively more stable.

discovery:
Lutetium was discovered independently in 1907 by three scientists: French chemist **Georges Urbain**,
            Austrian mineralogist **Carl Auer von Welsbach**, and American chemist **Charles James**. Urbain named it
            after **Lutetia**, the ancient Roman name for Paris. It was the last of the naturally occurring rare-earth
            elements to be discovered.
uses: Lutetium is used as a **catalyst in petroleum cracking** and in some hydrogenation processes.

Due to its stable neutron absorption, the isotope Lutetium-176 is used as a detector for **neutrino
                research** and in certain types of radiation detectors.

The radioisotope **Lutetium-177** is used in medical therapies for certain types of cancer, a field
                known as targeted radionuclide therapy.

It is also used as a component in certain **high-refractive-index glasses** and in ceramic garnets for
                specialized electronics.
interestingFacts:
Lutetium is the last element in the lanthanide series and is considered a d-block element due to its
                electron configuration.
It is the densest, hardest, and has one of the highest melting points of all the lanthanides.

Because of its very small natural abundance and difficulty in separation, lutetium is one of the most
                expensive elements in the world.
didYouKnow:
Lutetium's electron configuration, with a completely filled 4f subshell and a single electron in the 5d
            subshell, is a key reason why it is considered the end of the lanthanide series and the transition to the
            next row of d-block elements.

discovery:
