Magnesium oxide (“magnesia alba”) was recognized as a distinct substance by Joseph Black in 1755.
            Metallic magnesium was isolated in 1808 by Sir Humphry Davy through electrolysis
            :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}.
uses:
Alloyed with aluminum and zinc to create strong, lightweight materials used in aerospace and automotive
                industries
                :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}.

Burns with brilliant white flame; used in flares, fireworks, and photographic flash bulbs
                :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}.

Used medically as antacids (milk of magnesia) and laxatives, and to regulate nerve/muscle function
                :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}.

Used as a sacrificial anode to protect steel structures from corrosion
                :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}.
interestingFacts:
Magnesium ions are essential for over 300 enzyme reactions, including ATP processing
                :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}.

It is critical in the chlorophyll of plants for photosynthesis
                :contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}.

Magnesium has one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios among structural metals
                :contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}.
didYouKnow:
Magnesium played a key role in World War I lighting (star shells), and its production economy grew rapidly
            due to wartime need
            :contentReference[oaicite:12]{index=12}.

discovery:
Manganese was discovered by Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele in 1774, and first isolated by Johan
            Gottlieb Gahn later that same year.
uses:
Major component in steel production (ferromanganese and silicomanganese), improving strength, hardness,
                and wear resistance.
Used in aluminum alloys to improve corrosion resistance.
Manganese dioxide is used in dry cell batteries (alkaline and zinc-carbon batteries).
Manganese compounds are used as pigments, oxidizers, and in agriculture as a fertilizer component.
interestingFacts:
Manganese is essential for human health, playing a role in bone formation, metabolism, and antioxidant
                defense.
It gives amethyst its characteristic purple color.
Despite its importance in industry, manganese metal is quite brittle.
didYouKnow:
The largest reserves of manganese are found on the ocean floor in manganese nodules, which are potato-sized
            concretions containing various metals.

color: Unknown, but likely silvery-white or gray
discovery:
Meitnerium was discovered in 1982 by a German research team led by **Peter Armbruster** and **Gottfried
            Münzenberg** at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt. They synthesized it by
            bombarding a bismuth-209 target with iron-58 ions. The element was named in honor of the Austrian-Swedish
            physicist **Lise Meitner**, who made groundbreaking contributions to the discovery of nuclear fission.
uses:
Meitnerium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Meitnerium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Meitnerium-278, has a half-life of only about 8 seconds.
It is the first element to be named exclusively after a non-mythological woman.
Meitnerium is predicted to be one of the densest elements, with an estimated density of 37.4 g/cm³.
didYouKnow:
Lise Meitner's groundbreaking work on nuclear fission was crucial to the development of nuclear technology.
            The naming of meitnerium was a long-overdue honor for her significant contributions to science.

discovery:
Mendelevium was discovered in 1955 by a team of scientists led by **Glenn T. Seaborg** at the University
            of California, Berkeley. They synthesized it by bombarding a tiny sample of einsteinium-253 with alpha
            particles (helium nuclei) in a particle accelerator. They named it in honor of **Dmitri Mendeleev**, the
            Russian chemist who created the periodic table.
uses:
Mendelevium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the chemistry of the actinide series
                and to synthesize even heavier transuranic elements.
interestingFacts: Mendelevium was the ninth transuranic element to be discovered.
Its most stable isotope, Mendelevium-258, has a half-life of about 51 days.

It was the **first element to be named after a scientist** who was still living at the time of its
                naming.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of mendelevium was a major breakthrough in nuclear chemistry. The experiment was so
            innovative that it relied on identifying a single atom of the new element based on its radioactive decay,
            a truly remarkable feat of scientific ingenuity.

discovery:
Mercury has been known and used since antiquity. It has been found in ancient Egyptian tombs from as far
            back as 1500 BCE. Its properties were known to ancient Greeks, Romans, Chinese, and Indians. Its symbol, Hg,
            comes from its Latinized Greek name, *hydrargyrum*, meaning "**water-silver**," in reference to its liquid
            metallic nature.
uses:
Historically, mercury was used extensively in **thermometers, barometers, and sphygmomanometers** (blood
                pressure monitors). This use is now heavily restricted due to its toxicity.
It is still used in some **dental amalgams** for fillings, though this use is also declining.
Mercury is a key component in **fluorescent lights** and some other specialized types of lighting.
It is used in some chemical catalysts, particularly in the production of certain plastics.

The element's high density and liquid state have made it useful in certain industrial switches and
                relays.
interestingFacts:
Mercury is the **only metallic element that is a liquid** at standard temperature and pressure. Only
                bromine is a liquid non-metal.

It is a heavy, silvery-white liquid. Due to its high surface tension, it forms round beads when spilled
                on a flat surface.

Mercury is highly **toxic**, and its vapor is particularly dangerous when inhaled. Prolonged exposure
                can
                cause serious neurological damage and kidney problems.
didYouKnow:
The phrase "**mad as a hatter**" is believed to originate from mercury poisoning. Hat makers in the 18th and
            19th centuries used mercury compounds to treat felt, and the prolonged exposure to mercury vapor caused
            neurological damage, including tremors, shyness, and irritability.

discovery:
Molybdenum was discovered in 1778 by Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele in a mineral
            known as molybdenite. However, the element was first isolated by Peter Jacob Hjelm in 1781.
            The name is derived from the Greek word "molybdos," meaning "lead," as molybdenite was often confused with
            lead ore.
uses:
Used as a major alloying agent in steel and cast iron to increase strength, hardness, and corrosion
                resistance at high temperatures.
Molybdenum disulfide ($MoS_2$) is a key component in dry lubricants due to its low friction properties.
Used in high-temperature heating elements, furnace parts, and electrodes.
Molybdenum is an essential trace element in biology, playing a role in the function of various enzymes.
interestingFacts:
Molybdenum has one of the highest melting points of all pure elements, second only to tungsten and
                tantalum.
It is an essential element for plant nutrition and is often a component of fertilizers.

In its pure form, molybdenum is soft and ductile, but it becomes harder and more resistant to heat when
                alloyed with other metals.
didYouKnow:
The iron and steel industries account for over 75% of global molybdenum consumption. Its ability to enhance
            the strength and durability of steel at extreme temperatures makes it indispensable for components in
            industrial machinery, aircraft, and armor.

color: Unknown, but likely a metallic appearance
discovery:
Moscovium was discovered in 2003 by a Russian-American team at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research
            (JINR) in Dubna, Russia. The team was led by **Yuri Oganessian**. They synthesized it by bombarding a
            target of americium-243 with a beam of calcium-48 ions. The element was named in honor of the **Moscow
            region** and Moscow Oblast, home to the JINR laboratory.
uses:
Moscovium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Moscovium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Moscovium-288, has a half-life of only about 160 milliseconds.

It is located in the theorized "**island of stability**" and is predicted to have properties of both
                metals and metalloids.

Its discovery was a significant step in the synthesis of superheavy elements, and it helps to confirm
                the trends of the periodic table in this extreme region.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of moscovium involved a challenging experiment that required bombarding a tiny target of
            americium with a high-intensity calcium beam for months. This process produced only a handful of atoms,
            which were identified based on their radioactive decay.

color: Silvery-white metal with a yellowish tinge
discovery:
Neodymium was discovered in 1885 by Austrian chemist **Carl Auer von Welsbach**. He successfully separated
            the element from a material called didymium, which was previously thought to be a single element. He also
            discovered praseodymium from the same material. He named it Neodymium, which comes from the Greek words
            *neos* (meaning "new") and *didymos* (meaning "twin"), reflecting its discovery as the "new twin" to
            praseodymium and its relationship to didymium.
uses:
The most significant use of neodymium is in the production of **neodymium magnets**, which are the
                strongest and most widely used type of rare-earth magnets.

Neodymium magnets are essential in many modern technologies, including headphones, microphones,
                computer hard drives, and electric vehicle motors.

Neodymium compounds are used to color glass and ceramics in various shades from violet to red, and to
                create a special glass that changes color under different lighting.

Neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) crystals are a crucial component in high-power lasers,
                which are used in eye surgery, cosmetic surgery, and industrial applications.
It is also a component in didymium glass, used for protective goggles by welders and glassblowers.
interestingFacts: Neodymium magnets can be more than 10 times stronger than conventional iron magnets of the same size.

The beautiful violet-red color of neodymium glass is a result of the element's unique light absorption
                properties.

Neodymium metal tarnishes readily in air, forming a flaky reddish-purple oxide coating that doesn't
                protect the metal from further oxidation.
didYouKnow:
The high demand for neodymium magnets in consumer electronics, wind turbines, and electric vehicles has
            made neodymium a strategically important and valuable element, and its price can be quite volatile.

discovery:
Neon was discovered in 1898 by Sir William Ramsay and Morris W. Travers in London by studying liquefied air.
            They isolated neon by fractional distillation.
uses: Used in neon signs and lighting due to its bright glow when electrified.
Used in high-voltage indicators and vacuum tubes.
Used in cryogenics as a refrigerant.
Used in gas lasers and as a component in some plasma displays.
interestingFacts: Neon lights actually emit red-orange light; other colors are due to other gases or coatings.
It’s chemically inert and forms no stable compounds under normal conditions.
It is the fifth most abundant element in the universe.
didYouKnow:
The name “Neon” comes from the Greek word *neos*, meaning "new". Even though it's colorless as a gas, it
            glows brilliantly in electric discharge!

discovery:
Neptunium was discovered in 1940 by American physicists **Edwin McMillan** and **Philip H. Abelson** at the
            University of California, Berkeley. They produced it by bombarding uranium-238 with neutrons. It was the
            first transuranic element (elements with an atomic number greater than 92) to be discovered. They named it
            after the planet **Neptune**, the next planet in our solar system after Uranus, mirroring the element's
            position after uranium in the periodic table.
uses: Neptunium has **no commercial uses** outside of scientific research and specialized applications.

The isotope **Neptunium-237** is used as a target material to produce **plutonium-238** through a
                neutron
                bombardment process. Plutonium-238 is the fuel for **radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs)**,
                which
                power many deep-space probes.
It is also used in nuclear physics research to study the properties of actinides.
interestingFacts:
Neptunium is a very dense, hard, and highly radioactive metal. It is the first synthetic element that
                is an actinide.
It has an unusually wide range of oxidation states, which makes its chemistry complex.

Neptunium-237, with its half-life of 2.14 million years, is the most stable and longest-lived isotope of
                the element.
didYouKnow:
The power source of many famous NASA missions, such as the Voyager and Cassini probes, is an RTG that is
            fueled by plutonium-238, which is itself produced by neptunium-237. This makes neptunium a key, albeit
            indirect, element for human exploration of the outer solar system.

color: Lustrous, silvery-white metal with a slight golden tinge
discovery:
Nickel was discovered by Swedish chemist Axel Fredrik Cronstedt in 1751. He initially mistook a mineral for
            a copper ore, but later extracted a new metal from it, which he named nickel (from the German
            "Kupfernickel", meaning "copper demon" or "goblin's copper", referring to its deceptive appearance).
uses:
Primary component in stainless steel and other alloys (e.g., Inconel, Monel) for their corrosion
                resistance and high-temperature strength.

Used in coinage and as a plating material (nickel plating) for corrosion protection and decorative
                purposes.

Important in rechargeable batteries, particularly nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cd) and nickel-metal hydride
                (Ni-MH) batteries.
Used as a catalyst in various industrial chemical processes, such as hydrogenation.
interestingFacts: Nickel is one of only three naturally occurring ferromagnetic elements, alongside iron and cobalt.
It has good ductility and malleability, making it easily workable.
Around 20% of the nickel produced annually goes into plating applications.
didYouKnow:
Meteorites often contain a significant amount of nickel, sometimes as high as 5-20%, which is one of the
            ways to identify a meteorite from terrestrial rocks.

color: Unknown, but likely a metallic, silvery color
discovery:
Nihonium was discovered in 2004 by a team of Japanese scientists led by **Kosuke Morita** at the
            RIKEN laboratory. They synthesized it by bombarding a bismuth-209 target with a zinc-70 beam. The element
            was named after the Japanese word **Nihon** for Japan, and it was the first element discovered in Asia.
uses:
Nihonium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Nihonium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Nihonium-286, has a half-life of only about 10 seconds.

It is the heaviest known member of the Group 13 elements, and its chemical properties are
                expected to be similar to its lighter homologues, gallium, indium, and thallium.
The discovery and naming of nihonium was a major achievement for Japanese science.
didYouKnow:
The discovery and naming of nihonium marked the first time an element was discovered and named by a team
            in an Asian country. The name is a tribute to the nation of its discovery.

discovery:
Niobium was discovered in 1801 by English chemist Charles Hatchett, who named it columbium.
            In 1844, German chemist Heinrich Rose discovered what he believed was a new element and
            named it niobium after Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus in Greek mythology. It was later confirmed that
            columbium and niobium were the same element. The name niobium was officially adopted by IUPAC in 1949.
uses:
Used in high-strength, low-alloy (HSLA) steels to increase strength and toughness, particularly in
                pipelines and structural components.

A major alloying element in nickel-based superalloys for jet engines and rocket assemblies due to its
                high-temperature strength.

Niobium-titanium and niobium-tin alloys are superconductors used to create powerful magnets in MRI
                machines and particle accelerators.
Used in jewelry and some surgical implants due to its hypoallergenic and non-toxic properties.
interestingFacts: Niobium is a superconductor at low temperatures.
It is highly resistant to corrosion but will oxidize in air at temperatures above 400°C.
It can be anodized to produce a wide range of iridescent colors, making it popular for jewelry.
didYouKnow:
Niobium's use in superalloys for aerospace applications was crucial for the development of early space
            programs like the Apollo Service Module and is still used in modern rocket engines, such as those made by
            SpaceX.

discovery:
Nitrogen was discovered in 1772 by Scottish physician Daniel Rutherford, who removed oxygen and carbon dioxide
      from air and showed that the remaining gas could not support life or combustion.
uses: Used in the production of ammonia for fertilizers via the Haber process.
As a protective gas in food packaging to prevent spoilage.
Liquid nitrogen is used as a cryogen for freezing and storing biological samples.
Used in electronics, explosives, and welding.
interestingFacts: Nitrogen is essential for life — it's a major part of amino acids, proteins, and DNA.

Despite its abundance, nitrogen must be fixed (converted) into usable forms by bacteria or industrial
        processes.
It is extremely inert in its gaseous diatomic form (N₂) due to a strong triple bond.
didYouKnow:
Lightning can break the strong N≡N bond in atmospheric nitrogen, allowing it to combine with oxygen and form
      nitrogen oxides — a natural form of nitrogen fixation.

discovery:
Nobelium was discovered in 1958 by a team of American scientists led by **Glenn T. Seaborg**, **Albert
            Ghiorso**, and **Torbjørn Sikkeland** at the University of California, Berkeley. They synthesized it by
            bombarding a curium-246 target with carbon-12 ions. The element was named in honor of **Alfred Nobel**,
            the Swedish chemist who invented dynamite and established the Nobel Prizes.
uses:
Nobelium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research**, particularly to understand the properties of the actinide
                series and to produce heavier, transuranic elements.
interestingFacts: Nobelium was the tenth transuranic element to be discovered.
The most stable isotope, Nobelium-259, has a half-life of 58 minutes.

There was a prior, incorrect claim of discovery by a Swedish team in 1957, which was later retracted.
                The American team's work was the one officially recognized.
didYouKnow:
Nobelium is one of the more difficult synthetic elements to study. Its short half-life means that any
            experiments must be conducted very quickly after its production, often on a single atom at a time.

discovery:
Oganesson was discovered in 2002 by a Russian-American team at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research
            (JINR) in Dubna, Russia. The team was led by **Yuri Oganessian** and included scientists from the Lawrence
            Livermore National Laboratory. The element was named in honor of **Yuri Oganessian**, a leading scientist
            in the field of superheavy element research.
uses:
Oganesson has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements and the limits of the periodic table.
interestingFacts:
Oganesson is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Oganesson-294, has a half-life of only about 0.89 milliseconds.
It is the **last element in the periodic table**.

Although it is in the noble gas group, theoretical predictions suggest that due to **relativistic
                effects**, oganesson may be a semi-metal or even a solid at room temperature, which is a major
                departure from the properties of its lighter homologues.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of oganesson completed the seventh period of the periodic table, providing valuable data
            for a new generation of scientists to explore the chemistry of the superheavy elements and the limits
            of nuclear stability.

discovery:
Osmium was discovered in 1803 by English chemist **Smithson Tennant**. He found it in the black, insoluble
            residue left over after dissolving platinum ore in a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acid (aqua regia).
            He named it "osmium" from the Greek word *osme*, meaning "**smell**," because of the distinctive, pungent,
            and volatile odor of its oxide, osmium tetroxide ($OsO_4$).
uses:
Osmium is used in very hard alloys with other platinum group metals for applications requiring
                extreme durability, such as **fountain pen tips**, electrical contacts, and instrument pivots.

Because of its toxicity, **osmium tetroxide** is used as a staining agent for biological samples
                in microscopy, as it is effective at fixing and contrasting lipids.

Its extreme hardness and high melting point make it useful in certain specialized high-temperature
                and high-pressure applications.
Osmium has also been used in some high-performance magnets and electrical components.
interestingFacts:
Osmium is the **densest stable element** known, with a density of 22.59 g/cm³, just slightly higher
                than its neighbor, iridium.

It has a unique bluish-white appearance and is extremely hard and brittle, making it difficult to
                fabricate.

The volatile oxide of osmium, osmium tetroxide, is highly toxic and can cause serious damage to eyes
                and lungs. This makes the handling of osmium a hazardous process.
didYouKnow:
Due to its extreme hardness and resistance to wear, osmium was historically used in the tips of high-quality
            fountain pen nibs, especially the famous "Parker 51," to provide a long-lasting, smooth writing experience.

color: less gas; pale blue in liquid/solid form
discovery:
Oxygen was independently discovered by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in the early 1770s and Joseph Priestley in 1774.
            Antoine Lavoisier later named and characterized the element in 1777 :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}.
uses: Essential for respiration in living organisms and metabolic processes
Steel and metal production (oxy‑fuel welding and cutting)
Industrial synthesis (e.g., ethylene oxide, plastics)
Medical use in oxygen therapy and life‑support systems
Rocket propellant when combined with hydrogen

Liquid oxygen is used in cryogenics and rocketry due to its paramagnetic behavior
                :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}.
interestingFacts:
Oxygen is vital for life and is a key component of DNA, proteins, and sugars
                :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}

Liquid oxygen is pale blue and strongly paramagnetic—it can be suspended in a magnet’s field
                :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}

Auroras are caused by excited oxygen atoms emitting green and red light
                :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

Excess oxygen exposure can cause toxicity, especially under pressure environments such as diving—known
                as oxygen toxicity or convulsions :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}
didYouKnow:
Lightning naturally fixes atmospheric nitrogen into reactive forms—but it also produces highly reactive
            oxygen radicals used in ozone formation and natural chemistry cycles
            :contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}.

discovery:
Palladium was discovered in 1803 by English chemist William Hyde Wollaston. He found the
            element while working with crude platinum ore from South America. He named it after the asteroid Pallas,
            which had been discovered two years earlier.
uses:
Approximately 85% of palladium is used in catalytic converters for vehicles to reduce harmful exhaust
                emissions.
It is used in dentistry for dental fillings, crowns, and bridges due to its resistance to corrosion.
Palladium is used in jewelry as a part of white gold alloys and in fine watchmaking.

It is an important catalyst in various chemical reactions, including those used in the production of
                synthetic fibers and fertilizers.

Due to its ability to absorb large amounts of hydrogen, it is used in hydrogen purification and storage
                technologies.
interestingFacts:
Palladium is a platinum group metal that is notable for its unique electron configuration, being the
                only element to have a completely filled d-subshell and an empty s-subshell in its ground state.
It has the lowest melting point of all the platinum group metals.

Palladium can absorb up to 900 times its own volume of hydrogen, a property that makes it a key
                component in hydrogen fuel cell technology.
didYouKnow:
The price of palladium can be quite volatile and, at times, has exceeded the price of gold, particularly
            driven by demand from the automotive industry for catalytic converters.

discovery:
Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brandt—who distillated urine to isolate the glowing substance he
            called “cold fire.” The name means “light-bearer” in Greek. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
uses: Main ingredient in fertilizers (phosphates)
Red phosphorus used in safety matches, fireworks
Phosphor bronze in electrical components
interestingFacts:
Fourth most abundant element in living organisms (in DNA, ATP, membranes) ⬅ essential biochemical roles
                :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
Exists in several allotropes: white, red, black phosphorus
White phosphorus glows faintly in air and ignites spontaneously
didYouKnow:
Phosphorus was the first element discovered chemically (not known since antiquity). Brand distilled ~50
            buckets of urine to produce ~120 g of the element. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}

discovery:
Platinum was known and used by pre-Columbian peoples in South America for thousands of years. It was first
            described in Europe by Spanish naval officer **Antonio de Ulloa** in 1748, who found it in Colombia. He
            named it "platina," meaning "**little silver**," as it was considered an unwanted impurity in the silver
            he was mining. The metal's true value was not recognized until much later.
uses:
The primary use of platinum is in **catalytic converters** for vehicles to reduce harmful exhaust
                emissions, accounting for over 40% of its demand.

It is a major material for **jewelry** due to its natural bright white color, tarnish resistance, and
                durability.

Platinum is an excellent **catalyst** and is used in a wide range of industrial chemical processes,
                including the production of nitric acid, silicones, and high-octane gasoline.

Its biocompatibility makes it suitable for **medical implants** and surgical instruments, and platinum
                compounds are important **chemotherapy drugs** used to treat certain cancers.
It is also used in electronics for electrodes, electrical contacts, and hard drives.
interestingFacts: Platinum is one of the densest elements, at 21.45 g/cm³, making it nearly twice as dense as gold.

It is a noble metal, meaning it is highly resistant to corrosion and oxidation, even at high
                temperatures.
The total amount of platinum ever mined could fit into a cube roughly 25 feet on each side.
didYouKnow:
Because of its extreme resistance to corrosion and wear, an alloy of platinum and iridium was used to create
            the original international standard **meter bar** and **kilogram mass**, which were the world's official
            units of measurement for decades.

color: Silvery-white, tarnishes to a dull gray or yellowish color
discovery:
Plutonium was discovered in 1940 by a team of American scientists led by **Glenn T. Seaborg**, including
            **Edwin McMillan**, **Joseph W. Kennedy**, and **Arthur C. Wahl**. They synthesized it by bombarding
            uranium with deuterons (nuclei of deuterium, an isotope of hydrogen) at the University of California,
            Berkeley. They named it after the dwarf planet **Pluto**, following the trend of naming new transuranic
            elements after the planets Uranus (for uranium) and Neptune (for neptunium).
uses: The primary use of plutonium is as **nuclear fuel** in certain types of nuclear reactors.
The isotope **Plutonium-239** is the fissile component in many modern **nuclear weapons**.

The isotope **Plutonium-238** is used in **radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs)**, which are
                compact, long-lasting power sources for spacecraft and other remote equipment.
interestingFacts:
Plutonium is a highly radioactive and toxic heavy metal. Due to its radioactivity, it is warm to the
                touch.

It is an extremely dense element, only slightly less dense than gold, and can exist in six different
                solid phases (allotropes) with varying crystal structures and densities.

A common isotope, Plutonium-239, has a half-life of 24,110 years, making it dangerous for centuries to
                come.
didYouKnow:
Plutonium-238 has a half-life of 87.7 years, which means it continuously generates a significant amount of
            heat from its decay. This property makes it the ideal fuel for RTGs, providing a reliable power source for
            deep-space missions like Voyager, Galileo, and Cassini, which traveled too far from the Sun to use solar
            power.

color: Silvery metal (rarely seen due to radioactivity)
discovery:
Polonium was discovered in 1898 by the brilliant Polish-French scientist **Marie Curie** and her husband
            **Pierre Curie**. They isolated it from the uranium ore pitchblende, and it was the first element they
            discovered on their path to discovering radium. Marie Curie named it after her native country, **Poland**.
uses:
Polonium is a powerful **alpha particle source** and is used in anti-static devices for industrial
                processes and for cleaning dust off photographic film.

The heat-generating property of polonium from its radioactive decay is being explored as a compact,
                reliable heat source for **space probes** and other remote equipment.
Polonium has been used in spark plugs for vehicles, though this use is no longer common.
The element is also a subject of research in nuclear physics and radiation therapy.
interestingFacts:
Polonium is a **highly radioactive and toxic element**. Its most common isotope, Po-210, is extremely
                dangerous even in minute quantities and is fatal if ingested.

It is the only element that can form a simple cubic crystal structure, a unique property in the
                periodic table.

Due to its intense alpha radiation, a small piece of polonium-210 glows in the dark with a bluish
                light from the ionization of the surrounding air.
didYouKnow:
Polonium-210 has a unique property of generating a large amount of heat from its radioactive decay. A
            single gram of pure polonium-210 can reach a temperature of 500 °C and produces about 140 watts of thermal
            power, making it a very efficient and dangerous heat source.

discovery:
Potassium was first isolated by Sir Humphry Davy in 1807 via electrolysis of molten potassium hydroxide
            :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}.
uses: Main component in fertilizers (potassium salts) :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}.
Used in glass manufacture and soaps (potassium carbonate/hydroxide).
Potassium chloride used in medical injections and salt substitutes.
Used as coolant in nuclear reactors.
interestingFacts:
Highly reactive—reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen gas and heat
                :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}.
Name derives from “potash”; symbol K from Latin “kalium” :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}.
didYouKnow:
The bright yellow color of streetlamp sodium flame tests include potassium’s signature flame spectrum
            (~766 nm).

discovery:
Praseodymium was discovered in 1885 by Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach. He
            separated a substance known as didymium into two new elements: praseodymium and neodymium. He named
            praseodymium from the Greek words *prasios* (meaning "green") and *didymos* (meaning "twin"), due to the
            distinct green color of its salts and its close relationship to neodymium.
uses: Praseodymium is used to color glass and ceramics a distinct yellow-green.

It is a crucial component in **didymium glass**, which is used in welders' goggles because it absorbs
                the intense yellow light produced by sodium.
In alloys with other rare-earth elements, it is used to make powerful **neodymium-iron-boron magnets**.

It is used in carbon arc lights to produce a very bright, high-quality light for the film industry and
                projectors.
Praseodymium oxide is a component in some types of pigments and catalysts.
interestingFacts:
Praseodymium is a soft, malleable, and ductile metal that is resistant to corrosion in air, which is
                unusual for a rare-earth metal.

The beautiful green color of praseodymium compounds is a result of the light absorption by the f-orbital
                electrons.

The term "didymium," from which praseodymium was separated, is still used in some contexts to refer to
                a mixture of praseodymium and neodymium.
didYouKnow:
Didymium glass, which contains praseodymium, is not just for welders. It is also used by glassblowers and
            jewelers to protect their eyes from the bright yellow light of molten glass, allowing them to see their work
            more clearly.

color: Metallic, sometimes with a greenish or bluish glow
discovery:
Promethium was discovered in 1945 by American chemists **Jacob A. Marinsky**, **Lawrence E. Glendenin**, and
            **Charles D. Coryell** at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee. They isolated and chemically
            identified the element from the fission products of uranium fuel. They named the element after the Greek
            Titan **Prometheus**, who stole fire from the gods, symbolizing humanity's use of the power of nuclear
            fission.
uses:
Promethium-147 is used in **atomic batteries** for devices that need a long-lasting, low-power source,
                such as pacemakers and some scientific instruments.
It is a beta radiation source used in thickness gauges to measure the thickness of materials.

Promethium compounds were once used in a type of **luminous paint** for watches and signal lights, but
                due to its radioactivity, it has largely been replaced by safer alternatives.
In the past, it was used as a portable X-ray source for certain applications.
interestingFacts:
Promethium is the only lanthanide and one of only two elements below bismuth (the other being
                technetium)
                that has no stable isotopes. All of its isotopes are radioactive.
Due to its radioactivity, it glows in the dark with a faint greenish-blue light.

The atomic mass of promethium is often given in brackets, [145], to indicate that it is a synthetic
                element with no stable isotopes and that the number refers to the mass of the most stable isotope.
didYouKnow:
Promethium was one of the last elements on the periodic table to be discovered. Its existence was
            theoretically predicted years before its discovery, and the search for it was a major scientific challenge.

discovery:
Protactinium was discovered in 1913 by **Kasimir Fajans** and **Oswald Göhring**. They initially named it
            "Brevium" due to the short half-life of the isotope they found. The element was more thoroughly and
            definitively isolated in 1918 by **Otto Hahn** and **Lise Meitner**. They named it "Protactinium" from
            the Greek words *protos* (first) and *actinium*, as it was the radioactive element that decays into
            actinium.
uses:
Protactinium has **no practical commercial applications** due to its scarcity, intense radioactivity,
                and
                high toxicity.

It is used exclusively in **scientific research**, particularly in nuclear physics, to study its
                decay properties and the radioactive decay chains of heavy elements.
Protactinium-231 is used as a tracer to study ocean currents and sedimentation rates.
interestingFacts:
Protactinium is a very dense and highly radioactive metal. It is highly toxic, and its handling
                requires extensive safety precautions.

Its most stable isotope, Protactinium-231, has a half-life of 32,760 years, but all of its isotopes are
                radioactive.
It is considered one of the rarest, most expensive, and most difficult elements to work with.
didYouKnow:
Because of its high toxicity and intense radioactivity, handling even milligram quantities of protactinium
            requires a special glove box and extensive safety precautions. There are only a few laboratories in the
            world
            equipped to work with this element.

discovery:
Radium was discovered in 1898 by Polish-French scientist **Marie Curie** and her husband **Pierre Curie**.
            They isolated it from the uranium ore pitchblende after a long and difficult process of fractional
            crystallization. They named the new element "radium" from the Latin word *radius*, meaning "**ray**," in
            reference to its powerful radioactivity.
uses:
Historically, radium was used in **luminous paint** for watch dials, instrument panels, and clock faces,
                causing a continuous glow from its radioactivity. This practice was discontinued due to the severe
                health
                risks associated with radium exposure.
In medicine, radium was once used for **radiotherapy** to treat certain types of cancer.
Radium is also used as a source of neutrons for research and in medical radiation devices.
interestingFacts:
Radium is a highly radioactive alkaline earth metal. It is over a **million times more radioactive**
                than
                uranium.
When exposed to air, pure radium turns black due to the formation of its nitride.

The intense radiation from radium causes the surrounding air to glow faintly blue in the dark, a
                phenomenon that captivated the public after its discovery but was later understood to be a sign of
                its dangerous nature.
didYouKnow:
For a time after its discovery, radium was celebrated as a miracle cure and was added to many consumer
            products, from toothpaste to bottled water. This widespread use led to many cases of severe health problems
            and death, a tragic lesson about the dangers of radioactivity.

discovery:
Radon was discovered in 1900 by German chemist **Friedrich Ernst Dorn**. While studying the decay chain of
            radium, he observed that radium compounds emitted a new radioactive gas. He initially named it "radium
            emanation," and it was later isolated and confirmed as a new element. in 1923, the name was officially
            changed to "radon" to reflect its origin from the element radium.
uses:
Radon has very limited practical applications due to its high radioactivity. Historically, it was used
                in
                **radiotherapy** for treating some types of cancer.

It is primarily used today in **scientific research**, particularly as a tracer in hydrology to study
                the movement of groundwater and ocean currents.
Radon is also used in some laboratories as a source of alpha radiation.
interestingFacts:
Radon is a **colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas**, making it difficult to detect without specialized
                equipment.

It is the **heaviest of the noble gases** and is one of the densest known gases at standard temperature
                and pressure.

Radon is considered a major indoor air pollutant and is the **leading cause of lung cancer** in
                non-smokers. Its radioactive decay products can be inhaled and cause damage to lung tissue.
didYouKnow:
Radon gas naturally seeps into homes and buildings from the ground through cracks in the foundation.
            In poorly ventilated areas, it can accumulate to dangerous levels. Testing for radon is a common practice
            in many countries to ensure indoor air quality and safety.

discovery:
Rhenium was discovered in 1925 by German chemists **Walter Noddack**, **Ida Tacke**, and **Otto Berg**. They
            identified the element in platinum ores and the mineral columbite using X-ray spectroscopy. They named it
            "rhenium" after **Rhenus**, the Latin name for the Rhine River in Germany, as a tribute to their homeland.
            It was
            the last naturally occurring element with a stable isotope to be discovered.
uses:
Rhenium is a key component in **high-temperature superalloys** used for parts of jet engines, such as
                turbine blades, which must withstand extreme heat and stress.

A **platinum-rhenium alloy** is an extremely effective catalyst used in the production of high-octane,
                lead-free gasoline.

Due to its high melting point and resistance to wear, it is used in filaments for mass spectrometers,
                thermocouples for measuring high temperatures, and electrical contacts.
Rhenium is also used in X-ray machines and in some rocket engines.
interestingFacts:
Rhenium has the **third-highest melting point** of all elements (after tungsten and carbon) and the
                **highest boiling point** of any element.
It is one of the densest elements, exceeded only by platinum, iridium, and osmium.

Although it is an extremely hard and dense metal, annealed rhenium is very ductile and can be bent,
                coiled, or rolled.
didYouKnow:
Rhenium's high resistance to thermal creep (deforming under high heat) makes it an indispensable component
            in superalloys for modern jet engines. A typical jet engine contains about 3% to 6% rhenium in its turbine
            blades, making it a strategically important and valuable element.

discovery:
Rhodium was discovered in 1803 by English chemist William Hyde Wollaston in London. He
            isolated the element from a piece of platinum ore, specifically one that had been treated to remove platinum
            and palladium. He named it rhodium after the Greek word 'rhodon', meaning rose, due to the rose-red color of
            some of its compounds.
uses:
The primary use of rhodium is in catalytic converters for automobiles, where it helps reduce nitrogen
                oxide (NOx) emissions.

It is used as an alloying agent to harden platinum and palladium, making them suitable for high-wear
                applications.

Rhodium is electroplated onto jewelry and mirrors to provide a durable, highly reflective, and
                tarnish-resistant finish.

In the chemical industry, rhodium is used as a catalyst in processes such as the carbonylation of
                methanol to produce acetic acid.

Because of its low electrical resistance and stable contact resistance, it is used in some electrical
                contacts.
interestingFacts:
Rhodium is an exceptionally bright and reflective metal, making it an excellent choice for plating
                mirrors and jewelry.
It is highly resistant to corrosion and is not attacked by most acids.

Rhodium is considered the rarest non-radioactive precious metal, and its price can fluctuate
                dramatically due to market demand.
didYouKnow:
Because of its high value, there have been a number of thefts of catalytic converters from cars, primarily
            to get the rhodium, palladium, and platinum they contain.

color: Unknown, but likely a metallic, silvery color
discovery:
Roentgenium was discovered in 1994 by a German research team led by **Peter Armbruster** and **Gottfried
            Münzenberg** at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt. They synthesized it by
            bombarding a bismuth-209 target with a nickel-64 beam. The element was named in honor of **Wilhelm Conrad
            Röntgen**, the German physicist who discovered X-rays.
uses:
Roentgenium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Roentgenium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Roentgenium-282, has a half-life of only about 100 seconds.

It is a very dense element, with an estimated density of about 28.7 g/cm³, similar to osmium and
                iridium.

Roentgenium is the heaviest known member of the Group 11 elements, and its chemical properties are
                expected to be similar to its lighter homologues, gold, silver, and copper.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of roentgenium helped to extend the periodic table and confirmed theoretical predictions about
            the chemical behavior of superheavy elements, showing that the trends established for lighter elements
            continue to hold true even at the extreme end of the table.

state: Solid (but very soft and highly reactive)
discovery:
Rubidium was discovered in 1861 by German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav
                Kirchhoff. They identified it using a spectroscope, observing two distinct red lines in the
            spectrum of a mineral called lepidolite. They named it "rubidium" from the Latin word "rubidus," meaning
            "deepest red," referring to these spectral lines.
uses: Used in atomic clocks, providing highly accurate timekeeping.
In high-tech vacuum tubes and photocells, due to its ability to be easily ionized.
Used in some specialized glasses and ceramics.
Rubidium carbonate is used in the production of some optical fibers.
Rubidium-87 is a radioactive isotope used in radiometric dating of rocks and minerals.
interestingFacts: Rubidium is a highly reactive alkali metal and ignites spontaneously in air, forming rubidium oxides.
It reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen gas and a significant amount of heat.

It is one of the few elements that are liquid near room temperature, though its melting point is
                slightly higher than gallium.
Its flame test produces a distinctive purplish-red color.
didYouKnow:
Due to its strong photoemission properties, rubidium is used in "atomic clocks" which are among the most
            accurate timekeeping devices, losing only about one second in many millions of years. This precision is
            vital for technologies like GPS.

discovery:
Ruthenium was discovered in 1844 by Russian chemist Karl Ernst Claus at Kazan State
            University. He isolated the new element from the crude platinum ore that came from the Ural Mountains. He
            named it "ruthenium" in honor of Russia, from the Latin word "Ruthenia."
uses: Used as a hardener for platinum and palladium alloys to create wear-resistant electrical contacts.
In the form of ruthenium dioxide, it is a versatile catalyst in the chemical industry.
A small amount of ruthenium added to titanium can dramatically increase its corrosion resistance.

Used in some specialized applications such as pen nibs, and in a new application as the capping layer
                for extreme ultraviolet photomasks.

Some ruthenium complexes are being researched for use in solar energy and as potential anti-cancer
                drugs.
interestingFacts: Ruthenium is one of the platinum group metals and is known for its extreme hardness and brittleness.
It is resistant to most chemical attacks, including all acids.
Ruthenium can exhibit a wide range of oxidation states, from +8 to -2.
didYouKnow:
Adding a tiny amount of ruthenium to titanium can increase its corrosion resistance by a factor of a
            hundred. This property makes it invaluable for certain industrial applications where titanium's durability
            needs to be maximized.

discovery:
Rutherfordium was discovered in 1964 by a team of Soviet scientists at the Joint Institute for Nuclear
            Research in Dubna, Russia, and independently in 1969 by a team led by **Albert Ghiorso** at the University
            of California, Berkeley. There was a naming dispute between the two groups. The name **Rutherfordium** was
            eventually adopted by the IUPAC in honor of **Ernest Rutherford**, the "father" of nuclear physics.
uses:
Rutherfordium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to understand the fundamental properties of the heaviest
                elements and to test theories of nuclear and atomic structure.
interestingFacts:
Rutherfordium is the **first transactinide element**, marking the beginning of the d-block in the
                seventh period of the periodic table.
The most stable isotope, Rutherfordium-267, has a half-life of about 1.3 hours.
It is an extremely heavy element, with an estimated density higher than that of gold or platinum.
didYouKnow:
The naming dispute over rutherfordium was a significant event in the history of element discovery. The
            Soviet team proposed "Kurchatovium" after Igor Kurchatov, while the American team proposed "Rutherfordium."
            The IUPAC's final decision resolved the controversy.

discovery:
Samarium was discovered in 1879 by French chemist **Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran**. While examining the
            mineral samarskite, he found new spectral lines that indicated the presence of a new element. He named the
            element Samarium after the mineral, which itself was named in honor of **Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets**, a
            Russian mining engineer.
uses:
The most significant use of samarium is in the production of **samarium-cobalt (SmCo) magnets**, which
                are
                the second strongest type of rare-earth permanent magnets.

SmCo magnets are highly resistant to demagnetization and can operate at high temperatures (up to 700°C),
                making them essential for military technology, aerospace, and high-performance motors.

Samarium-149 is a crucial component in **nuclear reactor control rods** due to its very high capacity
                to absorb neutrons.
It is also used to dope calcium fluoride crystals for optoelectronic applications.
Samarium compounds are used in infrared-absorbing glass and in some phosphors.
interestingFacts: Samarium is a hard, brittle, and silvery-white metal that tarnishes slowly in air.

Samarium has a high neutron absorption cross-section, which is a key reason for its use in nuclear
                reactors.

The discovery of the mineral samarskite, and subsequently the element samarium, marked the beginning of
                the age of rare-earth element discoveries.
didYouKnow:
Samarium-cobalt magnets retain their magnetic properties at much higher temperatures than neodymium magnets,
            making them invaluable for applications like high-performance motors in aerospace or defense systems where
            operating temperatures are a concern.

discovery:
First isolated in 1879 by Lars Fredrik Nilson from minerals euxenite and gadolinite. Its existence had
            been
            predicted by Mendeleev in 1869 as "ekaboron" and named after Scandinavia.
            :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
uses:
Added (<0.5 %) to aluminium alloys in aerospace & sports gear: bicycle frames, baseball bats, high-intensity lamps. 
                :contentReference[oaicite:3]index=3
Used in metal halide lamps to simulate sunlight. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

Scandium-triflate serves as a Lewis-acid catalyst in organic synthesis.
                :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
interestingFacts: Exhibits a +3 oxidation state exclusively. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}

Its properties closely resemble rare-earth metals despite being in group 3.
                :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}
didYouKnow:
Lightweight like aluminium but far stronger—scandium remains too costly for widespread use, though Sc-Al
            alloys are prized for high-performance applications. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}

discovery:
Seaborgium was discovered in 1974 by a team of scientists led by **Albert Ghiorso** at the Lawrence
            Berkeley National Laboratory in California. They synthesized it by bombarding a californium-249 target
            with oxygen-18 ions in a particle accelerator. The element was named in honor of the American nuclear
            chemist **Glenn T. Seaborg**, a pioneer in the discovery of many transuranic elements.
uses:
Seaborgium has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Seaborgium is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Seaborgium-271, has a half-life of only about 2.4 minutes.

It is the first element to be named after a living person. The naming of the element sparked
                controversy, but the IUPAC ultimately made an exception to its policy and honored Glenn Seaborg.
Seaborgium is a very dense element, with an estimated density of about 35 g/cm³.
didYouKnow:
The naming of seaborgium was a significant moment in the history of science. Glenn T. Seaborg was a lead
            scientist on the discovery team and was still alive at the time the element was named, a rare honor that
            highlighted his monumental contributions to nuclear chemistry.

discovery:
Selenium was discovered in 1817 by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who named it after Selene, the
            Greek goddess of the Moon, due to its chemical similarity to tellurium (named after Tellus, the Earth).
uses: Used in glass manufacturing to decolorize glass or to impart a red color to glass and enamels.

Historically used in photocells and solar cells due to its photoconductive properties (its electrical
                conductivity increases with light exposure).
Important component in rectifiers and other electronic devices.
Used as an additive in stainless steel to improve machinability.

Essential trace element for human and animal health, crucial for antioxidant enzymes and thyroid hormone
                metabolism.
Selenium sulfide is an active ingredient in some anti-dandruff shampoos.
interestingFacts:
Selenium exhibits photoconductivity, meaning its electrical conductivity increases when exposed to
                light, a property that led to its early use in light meters and solar cells.

It can exist in several allotropic forms with different physical properties, including a red amorphous
                form and a gray metallic form.
Both too little and too much selenium can be detrimental to health.
didYouKnow:
The ability of selenium to convert light into electricity was crucial for the early development of "electric
            eyes" and played a role in the nascent field of television technology in the early 20th century.

Silicon is essential to modern electronics—not just the 20th century semiconductor age, but also in glass,

discovery:
Silver has been known since ancient times and has been used by humans for thousands of years. It is one of
        the "seven metals of antiquity" mentioned in historical texts, and its discovery is not attributed to a
        single person. It was first mined in Anatolia (modern-day Turkey) as early as 3000 BCE.
uses: Silver is widely used in jewelry and silverware due to its beauty and durability.

It is an essential component in photographic film and plates, although its use has decreased with the
            rise of digital photography.

Due to its excellent electrical conductivity, it is used in electrical contacts, circuits, and
            conductors.
Silver is used in mirrors and optical coatings because of its high reflectivity.

It has antimicrobial properties and is used in water purification filters, medical applications, and in
            some clothing.
interestingFacts: Silver is the best conductor of electricity and heat among all metals.
In ancient times, silver was often considered more valuable than gold in some cultures.
Silver tarnishes when exposed to sulfur compounds in the air, forming a black layer of silver sulfide.
didYouKnow:
Silver has powerful antimicrobial properties. Colloidal silver was historically used as an antiseptic and is
        still used today in some medical and water purification applications.

discovery:
Sodium was first isolated in 1807 by Sir Humphry Davy via electrolysis of molten sodium hydroxide
            :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}.
uses: Used as a coolant in some nuclear reactors.
Metallic sodium is used in high-pressure sodium-vapor lamps for street lighting.

Sodium salts like NaCl (table salt) and sodium carbonate are widely used in food, cleaning, and
                industry.
interestingFacts: Metallic sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife at room temperature.
Its atomic emission produces the bright yellow flame used in flame tests (~589 nm).
Excess sodium intake can raise blood pressure; yet it's essential in physiological function.
didYouKnow:
The name sodium comes from the Latin *natrium*; the element plays a key role in nerve conduction and
            fluid
            balance.

discovery:
Strontium was discovered by Scottish chemist and physician Adair Crawford in 1790, who
            identified it in a mineral from Strontian, Scotland. The element was first isolated by Sir Humphry
                Davy in 1808 through the electrolysis of molten strontium chloride.
uses:
Used to produce the brilliant red color in fireworks and flares (strontium salts like strontium
                nitrate).

Strontium carbonate is used in the manufacturing of cathode ray tubes (CRTs) for color televisions to
                block X-ray emissions (though less common now with flat screens).
Strontium aluminate is used in "glow-in-the-dark" pigments.

Strontium-90, a radioactive isotope, has been used as a power source in radioisotope thermoelectric
                generators (RTGs) for remote applications, though its use is debated due to its radioactivity.
Strontium ranelate is a medication used in the treatment of osteoporosis.
interestingFacts: Strontium metal is highly reactive and readily oxidizes in air, forming a dark oxide layer.
It reacts vigorously with water, similar to calcium, producing hydrogen gas and strontium hydroxide.
Its characteristic crimson red flame color is used as a qualitative test for the element.
didYouKnow:
While many alkaline earth metals play a role in biological processes, strontium is not considered essential
            for humans. However, its chemical similarity to calcium means it can be incorporated into bones, which is
            why radioactive strontium-90 is a particular concern as a fallout product.

color: Gray, heavy, and very hard metal
discovery:
Tantalum was discovered in 1802 by Swedish chemist **Anders Ekeberg**. He isolated it from a mineral sample
            found in Sweden. He named the element after **Tantalus**, a figure from Greek mythology who was condemned
            to stand in water and under a fruit tree, but could not reach either. This name was a reference to the
            element's "tantalizing" and frustrating difficulty in dissolving in acids.
uses:
The primary use of tantalum is in the production of **capacitors** for electronics. Tantalum capacitors
                are known for their small size, high capacitance, and stability, making them vital for mobile phones,
                laptops, and digital cameras.

Tantalum is used in **high-temperature alloys** for aircraft jet engines, nuclear reactors, and missile
                parts due to its high melting point and resistance to corrosion.

Because it is non-irritating and non-reactive with body tissues, it is used in **surgical implants**,
                such as bone plates and screws.

It is also used in laboratory equipment and in chemical processing applications where strong acids are
                present.
interestingFacts:
Tantalum is highly ductile and can be drawn into a fine wire. It is also extremely hard, making it a
                difficult material to work with.

The melting point of tantalum is the third highest of all elements, exceeded only by tungsten and
                rhenium.

Tantalum forms a passive oxide layer on its surface, which provides it with excellent resistance to
                corrosion.
didYouKnow:
The name "coltan" is a portmanteau of the two minerals that make up the ore, columbite and tantalite. The
            high demand for tantalum in consumer electronics has made coltan mining a significant, and sometimes
            controversial, industry in parts of the world with large deposits.

discovery:
Technetium was the first element to be artificially produced. It was discovered in 1937 by Italian-American
            physicists Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè. They analyzed a sample of molybdenum that had
            been bombarded with deuterons in a cyclotron at the University of California, Berkeley. Its name comes from
            the Greek word "technetos," meaning "artificial."
uses:
The radioisotope Technetium-99m is the most widely used medical radioisotope for diagnostic imaging,
                including bone scans and heart function tests.
Technetium compounds are used in corrosion-resistant products and as a metallurgical tracer.
Technetium metal is a superconductor at temperatures below 11.2 K.

It is also found in some S-type stars, which has provided valuable insights into stellar
                nucleosynthesis.
interestingFacts: Technetium is the lightest element with no stable isotopes. All of its isotopes are radioactive.
It has a chemical behavior similar to that of rhenium and manganese.
Technetium's presence in stars was a key piece of evidence that elements are formed in stars.
didYouKnow:
The primary use of Technetium-99m in medicine is due to its ideal properties for diagnostic imaging: its
            short half-life of 6 hours allows for a quick scan with minimal radiation exposure, and it emits gamma rays
            that are easily detected by medical cameras.

discovery:
Tellurium was discovered in 1782 by Hungarian scientist Franz-Joseph Müller von
                Reichenstein
            while he was investigating gold ore from a mine in what is now Romania. He initially suspected it was a new
            element but did not prove it. In 1798, German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth isolated the
            element and gave it the name "tellurium" after the Latin word "tellus," meaning "earth."
uses: Tellurium is used to improve the machinability of copper and stainless steel alloys.
In the form of cadmium telluride (CdTe), it is a crucial component in thin-film solar cells.

It is used in certain types of rewritable optical media, such as CDs and DVDs, due to its ability to
                change its electrical resistance when heated.
Tellurium is used as a vulcanizing agent for rubber and as a catalyst in various chemical processes.
In some thermoelectric devices, tellurium compounds are used to convert heat directly into electricity.
interestingFacts: Tellurium is a metalloid, having properties of both metals and nonmetals.

The atomic mass of tellurium (127.60) is higher than that of iodine (126.90), the element that
                immediately follows it in the periodic table. This is one of the few exceptions to the general rule of
                increasing atomic mass with increasing atomic number.

Exposure to tellurium or its compounds can cause "tellurium breath," a garlicky odor in the breath,
                sweat, and urine.
didYouKnow:
The name for the element "tellurium" comes from the Latin word for Earth, "tellus," and the element
            "selenium" (its close cousin) comes from the Greek word for Moon, "selene."

color: Unknown, but likely a metallic appearance
discovery:
Tennessine was discovered in 2010 by a Russian-American team at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research
            (JINR) in Dubna, Russia. The team included scientists from the Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Vanderbilt
            University. The element was named in honor of the U.S. state of **Tennessee**, home to the Oak Ridge
            National Laboratory and Vanderbilt University, which were key partners in the discovery.
uses:
Tennessine has **no commercial applications** due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and
                very short half-life.

Its sole use is in **scientific research** to further understand the fundamental properties of the
                heaviest elements.
interestingFacts:
Tennessine is a highly radioactive element with a very short half-life. The most stable isotope,
                Tennessine-294, has a half-life of only about 51 milliseconds.

It is the second-to-last element on the periodic table and is a halogen, but due to relativistic
                effects,
                its chemical properties are expected to be significantly different from other halogens.

The discovery of tennessine required a collaborative effort between laboratories in Russia and the
                United States, highlighting the importance of international cooperation in scientific research.
didYouKnow:
The discovery of tennessine, along with other superheavy elements, provided crucial evidence for the
            existence of the theorized "**island of stability**," an area where certain superheavy elements might have
            longer half-lives than predicted.

discovery:
Terbium was discovered in 1843 by Swedish chemist **Carl Gustaf Mosander**. He found the element as a new
            impurity in yttrium oxide, which he was studying from a mineral found at the Ytterby mine in Sweden. He
            named the element "terbium" after the village of Ytterby, which has given its name to four elements
            (Yttrium, Ytterbium, Terbium, and Erbium).
uses:
Terbium is a key component in **green phosphors** used in fluorescent lamps, color TV screens, and LED
                lighting. Its compounds emit a bright green light when excited.

It is a crucial component in the alloy **Terfenol-D** (Terbium, Dysprosium, Iron), which exhibits
                magnetostriction. This property is used in actuators, sonar systems, and sensors.
Terbium is used as a dopant in solid-state devices and in certain types of fuel cells.

Its unique luminescent properties make it valuable in **anti-counterfeiting** measures, as it can be
                used in phosphors that glow under UV light.
interestingFacts: Terbium is a soft, malleable, and ductile metal that is stable in air, forming a protective oxide layer.

It exhibits a strong green fluorescence when exposed to ultraviolet light, a property that is central to
                many of its applications.

Terbium is a component of Terfenol-D, an alloy that can change its shape with a change in a magnetic
                field, a property that makes it useful in devices like high-performance speakers.
didYouKnow:
The green color produced by terbium phosphors is one of the three primary colors (red, green, and blue)
            needed to create a full spectrum of colors on a television or computer screen.

discovery:
Thallium was discovered in 1861 by English chemist **Sir William Crookes**. He was using a spectroscope
            to analyze the residues left over from sulfuric acid production and noticed a new, bright green spectral
            line. He named the element "thallium" from the Greek word *thallos*, meaning "**green twig**," in honor of
            this distinctive line. The metal itself was isolated a year later, independently by both Crookes and
            French chemist Claude-Auguste Lamy.
uses:
Historically, thallium compounds were widely used as **rat poisons and insecticides** due to their
                effectiveness and lack of color or smell. However, this use has been banned in many countries because
                of the risk to human health.

In the field of optics, thallium is used in some **photoelectric cells** and in certain types of
                glass with a high refractive index.

The radioisotope **Thallium-201** is used in nuclear medicine for heart stress tests, to visualize
                blood flow to the heart.
Thallium compounds have been investigated for use in infrared detectors and superconductors.
interestingFacts:
Thallium is a **highly toxic heavy metal**. Its compounds are often tasteless and odorless, which made
                them a favored tool for poisoning in literature and criminal history.

It is a very soft and malleable metal, so soft that it can be cut with a knife. When first exposed to
                air, it has a bluish-white luster, but this quickly tarnishes to a grayish color.

One of the most famous symptoms of thallium poisoning is hair loss, which can be mistaken for other
                medical conditions.
didYouKnow:
Due to the extreme toxicity of thallium, its use in consumer products has been almost completely phased
            out. However, its radioisotope, Thallium-201, is a safe and invaluable tool in medical diagnostics,
            highlighting the distinction between an element's toxic properties and its useful nuclear properties.

discovery:
Thorium was discovered in 1828 by Swedish chemist **Jöns Jacob Berzelius**. He isolated the new element from
            a mineral sample found on an island off the coast of Norway. Berzelius named the element after **Thor**,
            the Norse god of thunder, reflecting its discovery in a Scandinavian region.
uses:
Thorium is being actively explored as a **nuclear fuel** for next-generation nuclear reactors.
                Thorium-based
                reactors are a potential alternative to uranium reactors as they are more efficient and produce less
                long-lived radioactive waste.

Historically, thorium dioxide was a key component in **gas lantern mantles**, where it produced a
                bright,
                white light when heated. This use has largely been phased out due to its radioactivity.

An alloy of thorium and magnesium is used to improve the strength and high-temperature resistance of
                aerospace components.
Thorium is also used as an alloying agent in welding electrodes and in high-quality optical glass.
interestingFacts:
Thorium is radioactive, but its most common isotope, Thorium-232, has a half-life of over 14 billion
                years,
                making it a primordial element that has existed since the formation of the Earth.
It is a soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes slowly in air, turning a gray or black color.

Thorium is the first element in the actinide series with a filling f-orbital, although its ground-state
                electron configuration is an exception to the general trend.
didYouKnow:
Thorium-based nuclear power plants have several advantages, including the potential for a more abundant fuel
            source and the production of less plutonium waste. This has led to renewed interest in thorium as a cleaner
            and safer long-term energy source.

discovery:
Thulium was discovered in 1879 by Swedish chemist **Per Teodor Cleve**. While working with a sample of
            the mineral erbia (the oxide of Erbium), he was able to separate a new, brown substance which he named
            "thulia." He later identified this as the oxide of a new element. He named it "thulium" after **Thule**, an
            ancient name for Scandinavia, the region where the element was discovered.
uses:
Thulium is used as the active medium in certain **lasers** for medical and industrial applications,
                particularly for surgery and cutting.

The radioactive isotope **Thulium-170** is used in portable X-ray devices for non-destructive testing
                and in medical diagnostics, as it does not require a large, external power source.
It is also used as a component in some magnetic ceramics and alloys.
Thulium has been investigated for use in military and meteorological laser applications.
interestingFacts:
Thulium is the second-least abundant of the lanthanide elements in the Earth's crust, with only
                the radioactive promethium being rarer.
It is a fairly soft, silvery-gray metal that is malleable and ductile.

Thulium's name is a poetic tribute to the discovery location, as "Thule" was a mythical place believed
                to be at the edge of the world.
didYouKnow:
The use of Thulium-170 in portable X-ray machines has revolutionized diagnostics in remote or emergency
            settings where traditional, heavy X-ray equipment is not feasible. This isotope provides a compact and
            reliable source of radiation.

discovery:
Tin has been known since ancient times and is one of the oldest metals used by humans. Its discovery is not
            attributed to a single person. It was a key component in the production of bronze, an alloy of copper and
            tin, which marked the beginning of the Bronze Age around 3000 BC.
uses:
Tin is most commonly used as a coating for other metals, such as steel, to prevent corrosion (e.g., in
                tin cans).

It is a key component in a variety of alloys, most notably bronze (tin and copper) and solder (tin and
                lead, or lead-free alternatives).
Tin oxide is used in ceramics and glazes to produce a white, opaque finish.

It is used in glass manufacturing to create float glass, where molten glass floats on a bed of molten
                tin to produce a perfectly flat surface.
Tin is also used in the production of organ pipes, bells, and other musical instruments.
interestingFacts:
Tin has a distinctive "tin cry" or "tin-plague" when it is bent. This is the sound of the metal's
                crystal structure twinning.

Pure tin can change its form (allotrope) at low temperatures. "White tin" (beta tin) is metallic, but
                below 13.2 °C, it slowly converts to "grey tin" (alpha tin), a non-metallic, brittle powder. This
                phenomenon is known as "tin pest."
The chemical symbol for tin, Sn, comes from the Latin word "stannum."
didYouKnow:
The use of tin in solder has changed significantly over the years. Due to health concerns about lead,
            lead-free solders, which are primarily tin-based alloys, are now standard in most electronics manufacturing.
